replace_subtopics.title: Boosting intuition: fit the residuals
replace_subtopics.body:
Start with the simplest prediction: the mean of the target for every row. Compute the residual for each row, which is actual minus predicted. The residuals show what the model still gets wrong.

Now train a small tree (a few levels deep) to predict those residuals from the features. Add that tree's output to the running prediction, multiplied by a learning rate such as 0.1 or 0.3. Recompute residuals and repeat. Each round nudges the model toward the rows it gets most wrong.

Why 'gradient'? For squared error, the residual is exactly the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the prediction. For other losses such as log loss for classification, the library fits trees to the gradient of that loss instead, so the same recipe works for yes or no targets, counts and rankings.

This differs from a random forest. A forest trains deep, independent trees in parallel and averages them to reduce variance. Boosting trains shallow trees in sequence, each depending on the previous ones, to reduce bias step by step.

A little history that interviewers still ask about: the first popular boosting method was AdaBoost (1995). Instead of fitting residuals, AdaBoost gives every training row a weight. After each small tree, it raises the weights of the rows that tree got wrong and lowers the others, so the next tree concentrates on the hard rows; the final model is a weighted vote of all the trees. Gradient boosting later generalised the same 'focus on your mistakes' idea to any loss function, which is why modern libraries use it and AdaBoost is mostly seen in textbooks.
replace_subtopics.example: A courier, Linthwaite Couriers, wants to predict delivery minutes from distance. The code below implements boosting by hand with depth-2 trees and learning rate 0.3. The training error falls from 6.74 after one round to 0.39 after 10 rounds and 0.16 after 30. The last number is below the noise level in the data (0.25), a sign that later rounds are starting to fit noise, which is why real projects watch a validation set.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, (300, 1))                       # e.g. distance in km
y = 3 * np.sin(X[:, 0]) + X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 300)   # e.g. delivery minutes

pred = np.full(300, y.mean())                          # round 0: predict the average
lr = 0.3
for round_ in range(1, 31):
    residual = y - pred                                # what we still get wrong
    stump = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2).fit(X, residual)
    pred += lr * stump.predict(X)                      # take a small step toward the fix
    if round_ in (1, 2, 5, 10, 30):
        print(f"round {round_:>2}: mean squared error = {np.mean((y - pred) ** 2):.2f}")

# Output:
# round  1: mean squared error = 6.74
# round  2: mean squared error = 3.87
# round  5: mean squared error = 1.11
# round 10: mean squared error = 0.39
# round 30: mean squared error = 0.16

replace_subtopics.title: Early stopping
replace_subtopics.body:
Guessing the right number of trees is hard, so let the data decide. Early stopping holds back a validation set, measures the loss on it after each round, and stops when it has not improved for a set number of rounds (the patience). The model keeps the trees up to the best round.

In scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting set early_stopping=True, validation_fraction and n_iter_no_change; recent versions also accept your own validation rows through fit(X, y, X_val=..., y_val=...). In XGBoost pass early_stopping_rounds and an eval_set; in LightGBM use the early_stopping callback. After fitting, check how many trees were really built (n_iter_, best_iteration, best_iteration_).

Two cautions. First, the validation set used for stopping has influenced the model, so still keep a separate test set for your final number. Second, for time-ordered data the validation rows should be the most recent ones, not a random sample, otherwise the model peeks at the future (see the timeseries topic).

Once early stopping has chosen the model, save it so the service that scores new rows uses exactly the same trees. For scikit-learn models use joblib.dump and joblib.load; for XGBoost and LightGBM prefer their own formats (booster.save_model('model.json') in XGBoost, booster_.save_model('model.txt') in LightGBM), which load across library versions more safely than a pickle. Write down the library version next to the file, because a pickle made with one scikit-learn version may refuse to load or behave differently in another. Finally, new rows must arrive in the same shape as training rows: same column names and order, and for categorical features the same pandas category dtype with the same categories. A region the model never saw is treated like a missing value, so log how often that happens. The mlops topic covers model registries and versioning in depth.
replace_subtopics.example: With a ceiling of 2,000 trees, learning rate 0.1 and patience 20, the model stops after 160 trees and scores R2 0.936 on the untouched test set, matching the best hand-picked setting from the previous grid at a fraction of the search effort.
replace_subtopics.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_friedman1(n_samples=3000, noise=1.0, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)

m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(
    learning_rate=0.1,
    max_iter=2000,             # a generous ceiling, not a target
    early_stopping=True,
    validation_fraction=0.15,  # 15 percent of training rows held back to watch
    n_iter_no_change=20,       # stop after 20 rounds with no improvement
    random_state=0,
).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print("trees actually built:", m.n_iter_)
print("test R2:", round(m.score(X_te, y_te), 3))

# Output:
# trees actually built: 160
# test R2: 0.936

import json, joblib, sklearn, numpy as np
joblib.dump(m, "boost_model.joblib")                          # save the fitted model
json.dump({"sklearn": sklearn.__version__, "trees": int(m.n_iter_)},
          open("boost_model.meta.json", "w"))                 # record the version beside it

loaded = joblib.load("boost_model.joblib")                    # later, in the scoring service
print("same predictions after reload:", np.allclose(loaded.predict(X_te), m.predict(X_te)))
print("saved with:", json.load(open("boost_model.meta.json"))["trees"], "trees")

# Output:
# same predictions after reload: True
# saved with: 160 trees

replace_subtopics.title: Key hyperparameters across libraries
replace_subtopics.body:
Beyond learning rate and tree count, a handful of settings do most of the work. They control how complex each tree is, how much randomness is injected, and how strongly large leaf values are penalised.

Tree size: max_depth or max_leaf_nodes (num_leaves in LightGBM). Boosting wants small trees, typically 15 to 63 leaves or depth 3 to 8. Minimum data in a leaf (min_samples_leaf, min_child_weight, min_data_in_leaf) stops tiny leaves that memorise rows. Row and column subsampling (subsample, colsample_bytree) train each tree on a random fraction of rows or features, which adds diversity like a forest and often helps. L2 regularisation (l2_regularization, reg_lambda) shrinks leaf values.

Tune in this order: fix learning rate at 0.1 with early stopping, tune tree size and minimum leaf size, then subsampling, then regularisation, then lower the learning rate at the end. Use cross-validation or a fixed validation set, and tools such as RandomizedSearchCV or Optuna when the search grows. The optional code shows XGBoost and LightGBM with the same ideas; it only runs if those libraries are installed.

Imbalanced targets. Fraud, churn and defect models often have 1 to 3 percent positives. Accuracy is then useless: always saying 'no' scores 97 percent or more. Judge the model with PR-AUC (average precision) and recall at a chosen threshold instead (see mlmetrics). To make the model pay more attention to the rare class, weight it: class_weight='balanced' in HistGradientBoosting and LightGBM (LightGBM also has is_unbalance=True), and scale_pos_weight in XGBoost, usually set to the number of negatives divided by the number of positives. Weighting mostly moves the probabilities up for the rare class, so more rows cross 0.5; it rarely improves the ranking itself. Often simply lowering the decision threshold on an unweighted model works just as well, and it keeps the probabilities honest.

Monotonic constraints. Sometimes the business or a regulator insists on a direction: more overdue days must never lower the risk score, and a higher income must never raise it. Trees can learn odd wiggles that break such rules on a few rows. All major libraries let you force a direction per feature: monotonic_cst in HistGradientBoosting (1 = can only go up, -1 = only down, 0 = free) and monotone_constraints in XGBoost and LightGBM. You usually lose very little accuracy and gain a model that is easier to defend.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer's claims-cost model at Oakhollow Mutual improved from R2 0.61 to 0.64 mostly by lowering max_leaf_nodes from 63 to 31 and raising min_samples_leaf from 20 to 100; the extra regularisation removed leaves that had fitted a handful of large one-off claims. Further tuning of subsampling added less than 0.005.

# pip install xgboost lightgbm
from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_friedman1(n_samples=3000, noise=1.0, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
X_fit, X_val, y_fit, y_val = train_test_split(X_tr, y_tr, test_size=0.15, random_state=0)

try:
    import xgboost as xgb
    m = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=4,
                         subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8,
                         early_stopping_rounds=20)
    m.fit(X_fit, y_fit, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], verbose=False)
    print("xgboost  best round:", m.best_iteration, " test R2:", round(m.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
except ImportError:
    print("xgboost not installed")

try:
    import lightgbm as lgb
    m = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.1, num_leaves=15,
                          subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.8, verbose=-1)
    m.fit(X_fit, y_fit, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)],
          callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(20, verbose=False)])
    print("lightgbm best round:", m.best_iteration_, " test R2:", round(m.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
except ImportError:
    print("lightgbm not installed")

# Output (with xgboost 3.2 and lightgbm 4.7 installed):
# xgboost  best round: 265  test R2: 0.941
# lightgbm best round: 180  test R2: 0.942

# Imbalanced target: 2.5 percent positives
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, recall_score
import numpy as np

Xc, yc = make_classification(n_samples=20000, n_features=8, n_informative=4,
                             weights=[0.98], flip_y=0.01, random_state=1)
Xc_tr, Xc_te, yc_tr, yc_te = train_test_split(Xc, yc, stratify=yc, random_state=1)
print("share positive:", round(yc_te.mean(), 3))
for cw in [None, "balanced"]:
    c = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(class_weight=cw, random_state=1).fit(Xc_tr, yc_tr)
    p = c.predict_proba(Xc_te)[:, 1]
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):<8} accuracy={c.score(Xc_te, yc_te):.3f} "
          f"PR-AUC={average_precision_score(yc_te, p):.3f} recall={recall_score(yc_te, p > 0.5):.2f}")

# Monotonic constraint: risk must never fall as overdue days rise
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
days = rng.uniform(0, 90, 2000)
risk = days / 90 + rng.normal(0, 0.15, 2000)           # noisy, but truly rising
free = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(days.reshape(-1, 1), risk)
mono = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(monotonic_cst=[1], random_state=0).fit(days.reshape(-1, 1), risk)
grid = np.arange(0, 91).reshape(-1, 1)
for name, mdl in [("free", free), ("monotonic", mono)]:
    drops = int((np.diff(mdl.predict(grid)) < 0).sum())
    print(f"{name:<9} places where more overdue days lowered the score: {drops}")

# Output (imbalance and monotonic constraints):
# share positive: 0.025
# class_weight=None     accuracy=0.987 PR-AUC=0.685 recall=0.58
# class_weight=balanced accuracy=0.966 PR-AUC=0.645 recall=0.76
# free      places where more overdue days lowered the score: 39
# monotonic places where more overdue days lowered the score: 0

replace_subtopics.title: Explaining predictions with SHAP
replace_subtopics.body:
Operations staff will ask 'why is this shipment flagged?'. Global importance charts answer 'what matters overall', but not 'why this row'. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) answers the per-row question.

The idea comes from game theory. Treat the features as players who cooperate to produce the prediction. SHAP gives each feature a contribution such that the base value (the model's average prediction over the background data) plus all contributions equals this row's prediction exactly. A positive value pushed the prediction up, a negative one pushed it down.

For tree models SHAP has a fast exact method called TreeExplainer. Common views are a waterfall plot for one prediction and a beeswarm or bar plot of mean absolute SHAP values for the whole dataset.

Limits to state clearly: SHAP explains the model, not the real world, so a large value is not proof of cause. Correlated features can split credit in surprising ways. And explanations of a poor model are explanations of poor reasoning. The shap library is optional; install it with pip install shap.

What about the built-in feature_importances_ bar chart? Be careful with it. 'Split' importance counts how often a feature is used in a split, and 'gain' importance adds up how much each split reduced the loss. Both are measured on the training data and both favour features with many distinct values, such as IDs or exact amounts, even when those features only help the model memorise. A safer, model-agnostic global check is permutation importance on a validation set: shuffle one column at a time and measure how much the validation score drops. A feature whose shuffling does not hurt the score is not really used for generalising, whatever the training-based chart says. In the code below features 5 to 9 are pure noise by design, and permutation importance correctly gives them about zero.
replace_subtopics.example: For one row, the model predicts 16.44. The average prediction (base value) is 14.0. Feature 1 adds 2.1, feature 0 adds 1.51, feature 2 subtracts 1.1, and the rest add small amounts. Adding them all to 14.0 gives exactly 16.44. In a dispatcher's screen this becomes: 'Flagged mainly because: Budgetship carrier (+), region R17 (+), long distance (+).'
replace_subtopics.code:
# pip install shap   (optional library)
import shap
from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

X, y = make_friedman1(n_samples=1000, noise=1.0, random_state=0)
model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X, y)

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)               # fast, exact method for tree models
sv = explainer(X[:5])                                # explain the first 5 predictions

row = 0
print("model prediction:", round(model.predict(X[:1])[0], 2))
print("base value      :", round(sv.base_values[row], 2))
print("contributions   :", sv.values[row].round(2))
print("base + sum      :", round(sv.base_values[row] + sv.values[row].sum(), 2))

# Output (requires pip install shap):
# model prediction: 16.44
# base value      : 14.0
# contributions   : [ 1.51  2.1  -1.1   0.27 -0.24  0.08 -0.04 -0.08 -0.05 -0.01]
# base + sum      : 16.44

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
model2 = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
pi = permutation_importance(model2, X_val, y_val, n_repeats=10, random_state=0)
print("drop in validation R2 when shuffled:", pi.importances_mean.round(3))

# Output (permutation importance):
# drop in validation R2 when shuffled: [ 0.393  0.453  0.123  0.658  0.143  0.001  0.001  0.001 -0.003  0.001]
checklist: Show per-row reasons in words staff use, not raw feature names
Pair SHAP with a global view so people see the usual drivers
Say plainly that contributions describe the model, not causes
Check a few explanations with a domain expert before release
Recompute explanations after every retrain; they change with the model

add_glossary: AdaBoost
An early boosting method that reweights training rows so each new small tree focuses on the rows earlier trees got wrong.
scale_pos_weight
XGBoost setting that multiplies the weight of positive rows, usually negatives divided by positives, for rare-class problems.
Monotonic constraint
A rule forcing the model's prediction to only rise (or only fall) as one feature increases.
Permutation importance
How much a validation score drops when one feature's column is shuffled; a model-agnostic measure of how much the model relies on it.
PR-AUC
Area under the precision-recall curve (average precision); a better summary than accuracy when positives are rare.
add_practice: On a synthetic fraud table with 2 percent positives, train a boosting model with and without class weighting, compare accuracy, PR-AUC and recall at threshold 0.5, then find the threshold that gives 80 percent recall on the unweighted model.
Add monotonic_cst so predicted risk can only rise with days overdue, check on a grid that it never falls, and report how much validation score you lost.
Save a fitted HistGradientBoosting model with joblib plus a small JSON file of library versions and column dtypes, reload it in a fresh Python process and confirm identical predictions.

replace_subtopics.title: kNN: distance and neighbours
replace_subtopics.body:
kNN does no real training. It stores the training rows. To predict, it measures the distance from the new row to every stored row, takes the k closest, and returns the majority class (classification) or the average value (regression).

The usual distance is Euclidean: square the difference in each feature, add them up, take the square root. Manhattan distance adds the absolute differences instead. For text embeddings, cosine similarity (the angle between vectors) is common; the embeddings topic covers it.

k controls smoothness. k=1 copies the single nearest row, so one mislabelled row changes predictions around it. A larger k averages over more neighbours and gives smoother, more stable boundaries, but too large a k blurs real differences. Choose k with cross-validation, and use an odd k for two classes to avoid ties. Neighbours can also be weighted by distance (weights='distance') so closer rows count more.

Because prediction compares against every stored row, kNN gets slow on large data and struggles when there are many features, since in high dimensions all points look roughly equally far apart.

At scale, nobody compares a query with every stored row. With a million rows or more, neighbour search uses an approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) index. The most common one is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): it links each point to a few close points in several layers, like a map with motorways on top and local streets below, and a search hops along the links toward the query. It returns almost always the true nearest neighbours (recall of 95 to 99 percent is typical) in milliseconds instead of seconds. This is exactly the machinery inside vector databases and pgvector, so kNN over embeddings and 'vector search' in the embeddings topic are the same idea at different sizes.
replace_subtopics.example: A garden centre chain, Mossgrove, wants to guess whether a customer will buy an annual membership from monthly visits and average basket in dollars. A new customer has 7 visits and a 50 dollar basket. Their nearest known customer is 5.4 away, and with k=3 the neighbours vote 2 to 1 for 'buys'. Notice the distances are driven almost entirely by basket size, because dollars span a much wider range than visits. That is the problem the next subtopic fixes.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

# known customers: [monthly visits, average basket in dollars], label 1 = bought the upgrade
X = np.array([[2, 20], [3, 25], [8, 60], [9, 55], [7, 70], [1, 15], [8, 40]])
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0])
new = np.array([7, 50])

dist = np.sqrt(((X - new) ** 2).sum(axis=1))    # Euclidean distance to every known customer
order = np.argsort(dist)                         # nearest first
for k in (1, 3, 5):
    votes = y[order[:k]]
    print(f"k={k}: neighbours {order[:k].tolist()}, votes {votes.tolist()}, "
          f"predict {int(votes.mean() > 0.5)}")
print("distances:", dist.round(1).tolist())

# Output:
# k=1: neighbours [3], votes [1], predict 1
# k=3: neighbours [3, 2, 6], votes [1, 1, 0], predict 1
# k=5: neighbours [3, 2, 6, 4, 1], votes [1, 1, 0, 1, 0], predict 1
# distances: [30.4, 25.3, 10.0, 5.4, 20.0, 35.5, 10.0]

replace_subtopics.title: SVM: the widest margin and the C setting
replace_subtopics.body:
A linear SVM looks for a straight line (or flat plane in more dimensions) that separates the classes. Many lines might separate them; the SVM picks the one with the widest margin, meaning the biggest distance to the nearest points of each class. Those nearest points are the support vectors. Only they define the boundary; moving any other point does not change it.

Real data overlaps, so SVMs use a soft margin: some points may sit inside the margin or on the wrong side, at a cost. C sets that cost. A small C tolerates many violations and gives a wide, calm margin with many support vectors. A large C punishes violations and gives a narrow margin that bends to fit individual points, which can overfit.

SVMs output a class and a distance from the boundary, not a probability. SVC(probability=True) adds a calibrated probability at extra training cost. Standard kernel SVMs train in time that grows faster than the number of rows, so they suit thousands to tens of thousands of rows. For very large or text data, LinearSVC or SGDClassifier are much faster.

More than two classes. An SVM draws one boundary between two groups, so a multi-class problem is split into several two-class ones. One-vs-rest (OvR) trains one model per class, 'this class against all others', and picks the class whose model is most confident; with 6 classes that is 6 models. One-vs-one (OvO) trains a model for every pair of classes and lets them vote; with 6 classes that is 15 models, each on less data. SVC uses one-vs-one internally, LinearSVC uses one-vs-rest, and you rarely need to change either.

Rare classes. If one class has far fewer rows, the margin gets pushed toward it, because violations on the big class cost more in total. class_weight='balanced' raises the cost of mistakes on each class in proportion to how rare it is, which usually lifts recall on the rare class at a small cost in precision.
replace_subtopics.example: On 400 points in two overlapping groups, C=0.01 uses 198 support vectors, C=1 uses 65 and C=100 uses 58. Test accuracy barely changes (0.94 to 0.96) here, which is common: C mainly changes how confident and how brittle the boundary is. Pick C by cross-validation on a log scale such as 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100.
replace_subtopics.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC

X, y = make_blobs(n_samples=400, centers=2, cluster_std=1.2, random_state=4)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=4)

for C in (0.01, 1, 100):
    model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=C)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    svc = model[-1]
    print(f"C={C:<5} support vectors={svc.n_support_.sum():>3}  "
          f"train={model.score(X_tr, y_tr):.2f}  test={model.score(X_te, y_te):.2f}")

# Output:
# C=0.01  support vectors=198  train=0.92  test=0.94
# C=1     support vectors= 65  train=0.92  test=0.96
# C=100   support vectors= 58  train=0.92  test=0.96

# Multi-class and rare classes
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score
X3, y3 = make_blobs(n_samples=400, centers=4, random_state=1)   # 4 classes
for shape in ("ovr", "ovo"):
    m3 = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(decision_function_shape=shape)).fit(X3, y3)
    print(shape, "models (scores per row):", m3.decision_function(X3[:1]).shape[1])

Xr, yr = make_blobs(n_samples=[950, 50], centers=[[0, 0], [2, 2]], cluster_std=1.0, random_state=0)
Xr_tr, Xr_te, yr_tr, yr_te = train_test_split(Xr, yr, stratify=yr, random_state=0)
for cw in (None, "balanced"):
    mr = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", class_weight=cw)).fit(Xr_tr, yr_tr)
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):<8} recall on rare class={recall_score(yr_te, mr.predict(Xr_te)):.2f}")

# Output (multi-class and class_weight):
# ovr models (scores per row): 4
# ovo models (scores per row): 6
# class_weight=None     recall on rare class=0.67
# class_weight=balanced recall on rare class=0.75

replace_subtopics.title: Naive Bayes for text with word counts
replace_subtopics.body:
Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule: the chance of a class given the words is proportional to the prior chance of the class times the chance of seeing those words in that class. The naive part is assuming each word appears independently of the others given the class. That is clearly false for language, yet the ranking of classes is often still right.

For text, first turn each document into word counts with CountVectorizer. MultinomialNB then learns, for each class, how often each word appears. To classify, it adds up the log probabilities of the words in the new text for each class and picks the highest. Smoothing (alpha, usually 1) adds a small count to every word so an unseen word does not make a probability zero.

It trains in one pass, works with a few hundred labelled examples, and is easy to inspect: you can list the words most tied to each class. Its probabilities tend to be too extreme, so use them for ranking rather than as exact odds. For higher accuracy on text, compare against logistic regression or LinearSVC on TF-IDF features, and against embeddings or an LLM when there is little labelled data.

TF-IDF, which the next models use, stands for term frequency times inverse document frequency. Term frequency is how often a word appears in this document. Inverse document frequency rewards rare words: idf = log(number of documents / number of documents containing the word). With 1,000 tickets, 'refund' in 10 of them gets idf = log(1000/10) = log(100), about 4.6, while 'the', found in all 1,000, gets log(1) = 0. So a ticket saying 'refund' twice scores 2 x 4.6 = 9.2 for that word, and 'the' scores nothing however often it appears. scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer uses a smoothed version, idf = ln((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1, so common words get 1 rather than 0, and then scales each row to length 1.

Naive Bayes comes in flavours for different data. MultinomialNB suits word counts. ComplementNB is a variant that learns from each class's complement (all the other classes) and is usually more accurate when classes are imbalanced, which help-desk queues nearly always are. GaussianNB assumes each numeric feature follows a bell curve per class, for measurements such as temperatures or amounts rather than words.
replace_subtopics.example: A software company's help desk has tickets labelled billing or technical. After training on 8 examples, 'where is my refund' comes out 93 percent billing. 'I was charged but the app shows an error' mixes both vocabularies and lands 78 percent technical, which is exactly the kind of ticket a human should double-check.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB

tickets = [
    "my invoice shows the wrong amount", "charged twice on my card",
    "refund has not arrived", "billing address is wrong on the invoice",
    "app crashes when I log in", "password reset email never arrives",
    "cannot log in after the update", "the page shows an error when saving",
]
labels = ["billing"] * 4 + ["technical"] * 4

vec = CountVectorizer()                      # turns each text into word counts
X = vec.fit_transform(tickets)
nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(X, labels)  # alpha=1 is add-one smoothing

new = ["I was charged but the app shows an error", "where is my refund"]
probs = nb.predict_proba(vec.transform(new))
for text, p in zip(new, probs):
    print(f"{text!r}: billing={p[0]:.2f} technical={p[1]:.2f}")

# Output:
# 'I was charged but the app shows an error': billing=0.22 technical=0.78
# 'where is my refund': billing=0.93 technical=0.07

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import ComplementNB
tf = TfidfVectorizer().fit(tickets)
idf = dict(zip(tf.get_feature_names_out(), tf.idf_.round(2)))
print("idf of 'the':", idf["the"], " idf of 'refund':", idf["refund"])   # 'the' is in 4 of 8, 'refund' in 1

cnb = ComplementNB().fit(tf.transform(tickets), labels)
print("ComplementNB on TF-IDF:", cnb.predict(tf.transform(new)).tolist())

# idf of 'the': 1.59  idf of 'refund': 2.5

replace_subtopics.title: Which one fits when
replace_subtopics.body:
None of these three is the default choice for most tabular business problems today; gradient boosting usually is (see the boosting topic). They still have clear niches.

kNN fits when similarity itself is the product: 'show me the five most similar past claims', recommendations by nearest item, or lookups over embeddings (where a vector database does the neighbour search). It needs scaled features, modest dimensions and enough memory to hold the data.

SVMs fit small to medium datasets with many features and clear margins, such as text classification with LinearSVC, or small scientific datasets with an RBF kernel. They need scaling and careful tuning of C and gamma.

Naive Bayes fits text and other count data when you need a baseline in minutes, have few labels, or need something tiny and explainable. It is also a good sanity check: if a large model barely beats Naive Bayes, question the extra cost.

One link worth making explicit: a linear SVM and logistic regression draw the same kind of straight boundary and differ only in the loss they minimise. LinearSVC and SGDClassifier(loss='hinge') minimise hinge loss, max(0, 1 - margin), where margin is the signed score times the true label (+1 or -1). A row that is correct and at least 1 unit past the boundary costs exactly zero, so only rows near or across the boundary (the support vectors) matter. Logistic regression minimises log loss, log(1 + e^(-margin)), which never reaches zero, so every row pulls a little and the output can be read as a probability. In practice their accuracy is often within a point of each other; pick logistic regression when you need probabilities.
replace_subtopics.example: Rookfield Legal routes incoming emails to 6 teams. Week one: MultinomialNB on word counts gives 84 percent accuracy in an afternoon. Week two: LinearSVC on TF-IDF reaches 89 percent. A kNN search over past emails powers a 'similar past matters' panel for the lawyers. Each model does the job it is best at.

import numpy as np
margin = np.array([-2, 0, 0.5, 1, 3])          # signed score x true label (+1 or -1)
hinge = np.maximum(0, 1 - margin)               # what LinearSVC minimises
logloss = np.log(1 + np.exp(-margin))           # what logistic regression minimises
for m_, h, l in zip(margin, hinge, logloss):
    print(f"margin {m_:>4}: hinge loss {h:.2f}   log loss {l:.2f}")

# Output:
# margin -2.0: hinge loss 3.00   log loss 2.13
# margin  0.0: hinge loss 1.00   log loss 0.69
# margin  0.5: hinge loss 0.50   log loss 0.47
# margin  1.0: hinge loss 0.00   log loss 0.31
# margin  3.0: hinge loss 0.00   log loss 0.05

add_glossary: TF-IDF
Term frequency times inverse document frequency: a word's weight is high when it is frequent in this document but rare across documents.
ComplementNB
A Naive Bayes variant that learns from each class's complement; usually better than MultinomialNB on imbalanced text classes.
GaussianNB
Naive Bayes for numeric features, assuming each follows a bell curve within each class.
One-vs-rest
Splitting a multi-class problem into one model per class, each separating that class from all others.
One-vs-one
Splitting a multi-class problem into one model per pair of classes that then vote.
HNSW
Hierarchical Navigable Small World, a graph index for fast approximate nearest-neighbour search used by most vector databases.
Hinge loss
max(0, 1 - margin); the loss a linear SVM minimises, zero for rows safely on the right side.

add_subtopics.title: Clustering text and embeddings
add_subtopics.body:
Today the most common clustering request an FDE hears is not about numbers at all. It is 'what are our 40,000 support tickets (or survey comments, or sales-call notes) actually about?' Nobody can read them all, and nobody has labels. The standard recipe has four steps.

1. Embed. Turn each text into an embedding vector with an embedding model (see the embeddings topic). Texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors, even when they use different words, such as 'money back' and 'refund'.
2. Reduce (optional). Embeddings have hundreds of dimensions, where distances become less informative. Reducing to 10 to 50 dimensions with PCA or UMAP often gives cleaner clusters and faster runs (see dimred).
3. Cluster. k-means is fine when you want a fixed number of themes for a report. HDBSCAN is popular for text because it finds the number of themes itself and puts odd one-off texts into a noise group instead of forcing them into a theme. Normalise the vectors to length 1 first so Euclidean distance behaves like cosine similarity.
4. Name. Cluster numbers mean nothing to a customer. Take 10 to 20 random members of each cluster, send them to an LLM, and ask for a short name and a one-line description. Then a human reads a few members of each cluster to confirm the name is honest.

Finally, report sizes and trends: 'Delivery tracking complaints: 18 percent of tickets, up from 11 percent last quarter' is the sentence the customer wants.
add_subtopics.example: Wrenfield Home, an online furniture shop, has 12 sample tickets in the code below. After embedding (TF-IDF plus TruncatedSVD stands in for a real embedding model so the example runs offline) and k-means with k=3, the tickets fall cleanly into refunds, login problems and parcel tracking, four each. With an API key set, the loop also asks an LLM to name each cluster from three sampled members. On the real 40,000 tickets the same pipeline produced 14 themes; the team merged two near-duplicates and renamed one after reading its members.
add_subtopics.code:
import os
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.preprocessing import normalize

tickets = [
    "refund not received for my order", "where is my refund for order 1182",
    "please refund the broken lamp order", "refund promised but my money never arrived",
    "cannot log in after password reset", "login fails and says wrong password",
    "password reset email never arrives so I cannot log in", "account locked after failed login attempts",
    "parcel tracking shows delivered but no parcel", "parcel tracking has not updated for five days",
    "courier left the parcel at the wrong address", "delivery late and parcel tracking stuck",
]

# Step 1: embed. In production call an embedding model (see the embeddings topic);
# TF-IDF plus TruncatedSVD stands in here so the example runs offline; it only
# matches shared words, while a real embedding model also matches synonyms.
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english").fit_transform(tickets)
vectors = normalize(TruncatedSVD(n_components=4, random_state=0).fit_transform(tfidf))

# Step 2: cluster (normalised vectors, so Euclidean distance follows cosine similarity)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(vectors)

# Step 3: sample members of each cluster and ask an LLM to name it
def naming_prompt(samples):
    joined = "\n".join(f"<ticket>{t}</ticket>" for t in samples)
    return ("Here are support tickets from one cluster:\n" + joined +
            "\nGive the cluster a short name (at most 4 words) and one sentence describing it.")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for c in range(3):
    members = [t for t, lab in zip(tickets, km.labels_) if lab == c]
    sample = [members[i] for i in rng.choice(len(members), size=min(3, len(members)), replace=False)]
    print(f"cluster {c} ({len(members)} tickets), sampled:", sample[:2])
    if os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"):          # only call the API when a key is set
        import anthropic
        client = anthropic.Anthropic()
        resp = client.messages.create(model="MODEL", max_tokens=200,
                                      messages=[{"role": "user", "content": naming_prompt(sample)}])
        print("   name:", "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text"))

# Output (no API key set, so clusters are not named):
# cluster 0 (4 tickets), sampled: ['password reset email never arrives so I cannot log in', 'account locked after failed login attempts']
# cluster 1 (4 tickets), sampled: ['delivery late and parcel tracking stuck', 'courier left the parcel at the wrong address']
# cluster 2 (4 tickets), sampled: ['where is my refund for order 1182', 'refund promised but my money never arrived']
checklist: Embed with the same model for every text, and store the vectors
Normalise vectors before k-means; try HDBSCAN when the number of themes is unknown
Sample members at random for naming, not the first rows
Have a human read a few members of each cluster before trusting the LLM's name
Report cluster sizes and change over time, not just names
Keep the noise group; odd texts are sometimes the most urgent

replace_subtopics.title: k-means step by step
replace_subtopics.body:
k-means needs you to choose k, the number of clusters. Then it repeats two steps.

1. Initialise: pick k starting centers, for example k random rows. The better default, k-means++, spreads the starting centers apart.
2. Assign: put every point in the cluster of its nearest center.
3. Update: move each center to the mean (average position) of the points assigned to it.
4. Repeat assign and update until the centers stop moving.

The quality score is inertia: the sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster center. Each assign and update step can only lower inertia or keep it the same, so the method always settles, usually within a few dozen iterations. It settles at a local best, not always the global best, which is why libraries run several random starts (n_init) and keep the lowest inertia.

k-means assumes clusters are roughly round and similar in size, and it uses distances, so features must be scaled first.

Using the segments later. A segmentation is only useful if next month's new customers can be placed into the same segments. Save the fitted scaler and the fitted KMeans together (a Pipeline does this) and call predict on new rows: each new row goes to the nearest existing center, and the centers do not move. Do not refit on the new data, or the segment numbers and meanings can change.

Very large data. Standard k-means looks at every row in every iteration. With millions of rows, MiniBatchKMeans updates the centers from small random batches (for example 1,024 rows at a time). Each step needs only one batch in memory, and partial_fit lets you feed it chunk by chunk from a file or database when the data does not fit in RAM. Its inertia is usually within a few percent of full k-means. Whether it is also faster depends on the machine, because scikit-learn's full KMeans is heavily optimised, so time both on a sample of your data.
replace_subtopics.example: The code implements k-means in NumPy on 150 points around three centres. Inertia drops from 1,349 after the first assignment to 222 and then 91, and the centers stop moving on the third iteration. The final centers land near the true group centres at (2, 2), (7, 3) and (4, 7).
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.vstack([rng.normal([2, 2], 0.6, (50, 2)),       # three loose groups of points
               rng.normal([7, 3], 0.6, (50, 2)),
               rng.normal([4, 7], 0.6, (50, 2))])
k = 3
centers = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]      # step 1: pick k random points as centers

for it in range(1, 11):
    d = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - centers[None, :, :], axis=2)
    labels = d.argmin(axis=1)                           # step 2: assign each point to nearest center
    inertia = (d[np.arange(len(X)), labels] ** 2).sum()
    new_centers = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) for j in range(k)])  # step 3: move centers
    print(f"iteration {it}: inertia={inertia:.1f}")
    if np.allclose(new_centers, centers):               # step 4: stop when nothing moves
        break
    centers = new_centers
print("final centers:", centers.round(1).tolist())

# Output:
# iteration 1: inertia=1349.0
# iteration 2: inertia=222.4
# iteration 3: inertia=90.6
# final centers: [[6.9, 3.0], [3.8, 7.0], [2.0, 1.9]]

# In practice: scaler + KMeans in one pipeline, then place new rows
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, MiniBatchKMeans
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

seg = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=1)).fit(X)
new_rows = np.array([[2.1, 1.8], [6.5, 3.4]])
print("segments for new rows:", seg.predict(new_rows).tolist())   # centers stay fixed

mb = MiniBatchKMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=1, n_init=3)
for chunk in np.array_split(np.vstack([X] * 200), 30):            # 30,000 rows fed in 30 chunks
    mb.partial_fit(chunk)                                          # only one chunk in memory at a time
full = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=1).fit(X)
print("full k-means centers :", sorted(full.cluster_centers_.round(1).tolist()))
print("mini-batch centers   :", sorted(mb.cluster_centers_.round(1).tolist()))

# Output:
# segments for new rows: [2, 0]
# full k-means centers : [[2.0, 1.9], [3.8, 7.0], [6.9, 3.0]]
# mini-batch centers   : [[2.0, 1.9], [3.8, 7.0], [6.9, 3.0]]

replace_subtopics.title: DBSCAN: clusters as dense regions
replace_subtopics.body:
DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) does not need k. It has two settings: eps, a radius, and min_samples, the number of points needed within that radius.

A core point has at least min_samples neighbours within eps. Clusters grow by linking core points that are within eps of each other, and by attaching border points that are near a core point. Anything else is noise and gets the label -1.

This lets DBSCAN find clusters of any shape, such as curved bands, and flags outliers for free. Its weakness is that one eps must suit the whole dataset, so clusters with very different densities are hard. A common way to choose eps is to plot each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour, sorted, and pick the value at the bend. Scale features first, as always with distances. HDBSCAN (in scikit-learn as sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN) relaxes the single-eps limit and is worth trying when densities vary.

Soft clustering with Gaussian mixtures. k-means, DBSCAN and hierarchical clustering give every row exactly one label. Real customers often sit between segments. A Gaussian mixture model (GaussianMixture in scikit-learn) assumes the data comes from k overlapping bell-shaped clouds, each allowed its own size and stretched oval shape, and gives each row a probability of belonging to each cloud, for example 0.55 'bargain hunter' and 0.45 'loyal regular'. That is useful for targeting (only send the loyalty offer when the probability is above 0.8) and for spotting borderline rows. You still choose k, and BIC (a score that rewards fit and penalises extra parameters; lower is better) helps compare values.
replace_subtopics.example: Two interlocking half-moons plus 3 stray points. k-means with k=2 cuts straight across the moons (agreement score 0.26, where 1.0 is perfect). DBSCAN with eps 0.2 and min_samples 5 recovers both moons exactly (1.0) and labels all 3 stray points as noise. In a fraud setting those stray points are often the most interesting rows.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

X, true = make_moons(n_samples=400, noise=0.06, random_state=2)
X = np.vstack([X, [[2.5, 1.5], [-1.5, -0.8], [0.5, 1.6]]])     # add 3 odd points
true = np.append(true, [-1, -1, -1])

km = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=2).fit(X)
db = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5).fit(X)

print("k-means agreement with the true moons:", round(adjusted_rand_score(true[:400], km.labels_[:400]), 2))
print("DBSCAN agreement with the true moons :", round(adjusted_rand_score(true[:400], db.labels_[:400]), 2))
print("DBSCAN clusters found:", len(set(db.labels_) - {-1}), " noise points:", (db.labels_ == -1).sum())
print("labels of the 3 odd points:", db.labels_[-3:].tolist())   # -1 means noise

# Output:
# k-means agreement with the true moons: 0.26
# DBSCAN agreement with the true moons : 1.0
# DBSCAN clusters found: 2  noise points: 3
# labels of the 3 odd points: [-1, -1, -1]

from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
Xg, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=500, centers=[[0, 0], [3, 0]], cluster_std=1.0, random_state=0)
gm = GaussianMixture(n_components=2, random_state=0).fit(Xg)
probs = gm.predict_proba(np.array([[-1.0, 0], [1.5, 0], [4.0, 0]]))
for x, p in zip([-1.0, 1.5, 4.0], probs.round(2)):
    print(f"point at x={x}: probability of each segment {p.tolist()}")
print("BIC for k=1,2,3:", [round(GaussianMixture(k, random_state=0).fit(Xg).bic(Xg)) for k in (1, 2, 3)])

# Output (Gaussian mixture):
# point at x=-1.0: probability of each segment [1.0, 0.0]
# point at x=1.5: probability of each segment [0.4, 0.6]
# point at x=4.0: probability of each segment [0.0, 1.0]
# BIC for k=1,2,3: [3444, 3401, 3438]

replace_subtopics.title: Pitfalls to avoid
replace_subtopics.body:
Clustering always returns clusters, even on random data with no real groups. That makes it easy to fool yourself and your customer.

The biggest technical traps are unscaled features, skewed features that let a few extreme rows drive the result, and too many features, which make distances meaningless (consider selecting features or reducing dimensions first; see dimred). Categorical columns do not fit k-means well; one-hot encoding them inflates distances oddly, and methods such as k-prototypes or Gower distance exist for mixed data.

The biggest process traps are treating clusters as facts rather than a useful simplification, reporting cluster ids instead of profiles, and never checking stability. Rerun with different seeds and on a different month of data. If customers jump between segments, the segments are not solid enough to plan campaigns around. Finally, judge clusters by use: do different segments respond differently to the actions you planned?

Track segment drift before campaigns rely on it. Customers change and so does the business, so a segmentation built in January can quietly stop matching reality. Each month, score everyone with the saved model and watch two things. First, the share of customers per segment: if 'lapsed' grows from 20 to 35 percent, something changed, in the customers or in the data feed. Second, a migration matrix: a table of last month's segment against this month's segment for the same customers. Most customers should stay put (a strong diagonal). Large flows between two segments are either a real change worth telling the business about or a sign the segments are not stable enough to plan around. When drift is large, refit, rename the segments from fresh profiles, and tell the teams that use them.
replace_subtopics.example: Tannerbrook, an online bookshop, first clustered on raw spend and visit counts. One segment contained 12 customers who were actually libraries buying in bulk; everyone else was lumped together. After a log transform, scaling and a separate rule to pull out institutional buyers, the remaining segments were stable across two quarters of data.

A faster k-means that updates centers from small random batches of rows, for millions of rows.

replace_subtopics.title: PCA intuition: the direction of most spread
replace_subtopics.body:
Picture the height and weight of 300 people as a cloud of dots. The cloud is a long, tilted oval, because taller people tend to be heavier. PCA asks: if I could draw only one line through the cloud and describe each person by where they sit along it, which line keeps the most information? The answer is the long axis of the oval. That line is the first principal component (PC1). The second component (PC2) sits at a right angle to it and captures what is left.

The maths, gently. First centre each column by subtracting its mean. Then compute the covariance matrix, a small table saying how each pair of columns moves together. Its eigenvectors are the directions of the oval's axes, and its eigenvalues are the variance (spread) along each one. Sort by eigenvalue, biggest first, and you have the components in order of importance.

Each component is a weighted mix of the original columns. Here PC1 is roughly 0.67 x height + 0.74 x weight, a 'body size' score. The sign is arbitrary: a library may return -0.67 and -0.74, which is the same line pointing the other way.

Going back, and why it matters. PCA can also run in reverse: inverse_transform takes the kept components and rebuilds an approximate original row. With all components the rebuild is perfect; with fewer it keeps the main pattern and loses the rest. The gap between a row and its rebuild is its reconstruction error. For normal rows that follow the usual pattern (tall people are heavier) the error is small. A row that breaks the pattern, say 190 cm and 50 kg, cannot be rebuilt from 'body size' alone, so its error is large. That makes reconstruction error a simple anomaly score for correlated data such as sensor readings, and the anomaly topic uses exactly this idea.
replace_subtopics.example: The code builds the height and weight cloud, finds the axes by hand with numpy and checks the answer against scikit-learn. Both find the same first axis, and PC1 holds about 94 percent of the variance, so one number per person describes this data almost as well as two. The widget on this page lets you change how tightly the two columns are linked and watch that share move.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
height = rng.normal(170, 10, 300)                   # cm
weight = 0.9 * height - 85 + rng.normal(0, 5, 300)  # kg, tied to height
X = np.column_stack([height, weight])

Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)                  # 1. centre each column at zero
cov = np.cov(Xc, rowvar=False)           # 2. 2x2 covariance matrix
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)         # 3. eigenvalues = variance along each axis
order = vals.argsort()[::-1]             #    sort biggest first
vals, vecs = vals[order], vecs[:, order]
print("share of variance:", np.round(vals / vals.sum(), 3))
print("first axis (by hand):", np.round(vecs[:, 0], 3))

pca = PCA(n_components=2).fit(X)         # scikit-learn does the same steps
print("first axis (sklearn):", np.round(pca.components_[0], 3))
print("explained_variance_ratio_:", np.round(pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 3))

# Output:
# share of variance: [0.938 0.062]
# first axis (by hand): [0.673 0.74 ]
# first axis (sklearn): [0.673 0.74 ]
# explained_variance_ratio_: [0.938 0.062]

# Rebuild from PC1 only and measure reconstruction error
pca1 = PCA(n_components=1).fit(X)
odd = np.array([[190.0, 50.0]])                       # tall but very light: breaks the pattern
typical = np.array([[180.0, 77.0]])
for name, row in [("typical", typical), ("odd", odd)]:
    rebuilt = pca1.inverse_transform(pca1.transform(row))
    err = np.linalg.norm(row - rebuilt)
    print(f"{name:<8} rebuilt as {rebuilt.round(1).tolist()[0]}  error {err:.1f}")

# Output (reconstruction error):
# typical  rebuilt as [178.9, 78.0]  error 1.5
# odd      rebuilt as [170.0, 68.2]  error 27.1

replace_subtopics.title: Explained variance and choosing k
replace_subtopics.body:
The attribute explained_variance_ratio_ lists the share of total variance each component holds. Add them up in order (a cumulative sum) and you get a curve that rises quickly and then flattens. You choose k, the number of components to keep, where the curve is high enough for your purpose.

The table shows the usual rules. In scikit-learn you can also pass a fraction, PCA(n_components=0.90), and it picks k for you.

Remember what variance means here: spread, which is not the same as usefulness. A small component can still carry the signal that separates fraud from normal. Explained variance tells you how much of the data's shape you kept, not how much predictive power you kept.

One warning about the numbers you will see in different places: scaling changes the answer. On the raw digit pixels, 21 components reach 90 percent. If you first standardise every pixel (StandardScaler), 31 are needed, which is the figure the animation on this page uses. Neither is wrong. Raw pixels let the busy central pixels dominate the variance, while standardising gives every pixel, including nearly blank edge pixels, an equal say, so more components are needed to cover them. Always state whether the data was scaled when you quote 'k components keep 90 percent'.
replace_subtopics.example: The digits dataset has 1,797 handwritten digits, each an 8 by 8 image, so 64 pixel columns. Two components keep only 29 percent of the variance: enough for a rough picture and little else. Twenty-one components keep 90 percent, so a team storing millions of such images could cut storage by about two thirds and still keep most of the detail.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)       # 1,797 images of 8x8 = 64 pixels
pca = PCA().fit(X)                        # keep all 64 components for now
cum = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)

for k in [2, 10, 20, 30]:
    print(f"{k:>2} components keep {cum[k-1]:.0%} of the variance")
k90 = int(np.argmax(cum >= 0.90)) + 1     # first k that reaches 90 percent
print("components needed for 90%:", k90)

pca90 = PCA(n_components=0.90).fit(X)     # or ask sklearn for the 90% cut directly
print("sklearn picked:", pca90.n_components_)

# Output:
#  2 components keep 29% of the variance
# 10 components keep 74% of the variance
# 20 components keep 89% of the variance
# 30 components keep 96% of the variance
# components needed for 90%: 21
# sklearn picked: 21

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
print("after standardising, components for 90%:", PCA(n_components=0.90).fit(Xs).n_components_)

# Output (scaled):
# after standardising, components for 90%: 31

replace_subtopics.title: Using PCA before a model
replace_subtopics.body:
PCA is often one step in a pipeline: scale the columns, reduce with PCA, then train a model on the components. Good reasons: many strongly correlated columns (50 sensors that all measure the same vibration), a model that is slow or unstable with many columns, or a need to shrink data.

Three rules keep it honest. Scale first: PCA follows variance, so a column in pounds with values in the thousands swamps a column in percent unless you standardise. Fit PCA on the training rows only, inside a Pipeline, so no information from the test rows leaks into the components. And compare against the same model without PCA, because on many tabular problems tree models such as gradient boosting (see boosting) do better on the raw columns.

The cost is interpretability. A component is a blend of dozens of columns, so 'PC3 raised the risk score' is hard to explain. If people must understand the model, prefer selecting a few original columns.

Text is a special case. A TF-IDF matrix (see knnsvm) has one column per word, often 50,000 columns, and is sparse: almost every value is zero, so it is stored as a list of the few non-zero values. PCA must first centre every column by subtracting its mean, which turns all those zeros into non-zero numbers and makes the matrix too big for memory. TruncatedSVD does the same kind of reduction without centring, so it works directly on the sparse matrix. Applied to TF-IDF it is known as LSA (latent semantic analysis): the components become loose 'topics' of words that appear together. It is a quick, cheap baseline for text features, though embeddings from a language model usually capture meaning better.
replace_subtopics.example: The code trains logistic regression on the digits with 5, 10 and 20 components and with all 64 pixels. Test accuracy climbs from 0.815 to 0.952 as k grows, and the full 64 pixels still win at 0.972. On this small dataset PCA buys smaller, faster data at a cost of about two points of accuracy. That trade-off is the conversation to have with the customer.
replace_subtopics.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)

for k in [5, 10, 20, None]:               # None = no PCA, all 64 pixels
    steps = [StandardScaler()]
    if k:
        steps.append(PCA(n_components=k, random_state=0))
    steps.append(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))
    model = make_pipeline(*steps)         # PCA is fitted on the training rows only
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{'all 64' if k is None else k:>6} features: test accuracy {model.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")

# Output:
#      5 features: test accuracy 0.815
#     10 features: test accuracy 0.876
#     20 features: test accuracy 0.952
# all 64 features: test accuracy 0.972

from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
docs = ["refund for my order", "order refund please", "login password reset",
        "reset my login", "parcel tracking late", "late parcel delivery"]
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(docs)          # sparse: mostly zeros
print("TF-IDF shape:", tfidf.shape, " non-zero values:", tfidf.nnz)
lsa = TruncatedSVD(n_components=3, random_state=0).fit(tfidf)
print("each document as 3 numbers:", lsa.transform(tfidf).shape)

# Output (TruncatedSVD on sparse text):
# TF-IDF shape: (6, 12)  non-zero values: 19
# each document as 3 numbers: (6, 3)

replace_subtopics.title: t-SNE and UMAP for visualising embeddings
replace_subtopics.body:
PCA draws straight lines, so it cannot unroll curved or tangled structure. t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding) and UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) are nonlinear methods built for one job: placing each row as a dot on a 2D map so that rows which are neighbours in the original space stay neighbours on the map.

They are popular for embeddings, the long lists of numbers (often 768 or 1,536 values) that language models produce for each piece of text (see embeddings). A map of support-ticket embeddings coloured by product quickly shows whether topics group together and which tickets sit in the wrong group.

The main knob in t-SNE is perplexity, roughly how many neighbours each point pays attention to (commonly 5 to 50). In UMAP it is n_neighbors, plus min_dist for how tightly points pack. t-SNE ships with scikit-learn; UMAP lives in the separate umap-learn package and is usually faster on large data. A common recipe for big embeddings is PCA to about 50 dimensions first, then t-SNE or UMAP down to 2.

In production, the more common reason to reduce embeddings is not a picture but storage and speed. A million documents at 1,536 float numbers each take about 6 GB, and search time grows with the dimension. Two options avoid a separate PCA step. Many embedding APIs accept a dimensions (or output dimension) parameter and return shorter vectors directly. Models trained as Matryoshka embeddings pack the most important information into the first numbers, so you can simply keep the first 256 or 512 values and re-normalise them, often losing only a little search quality. Always check the loss with a recall test on your own queries before switching (see embeddings).
replace_subtopics.example: The code maps the 1,797 digit images to 2D with t-SNE. For 98.8 percent of images, the closest dot on the map is the same digit, so the map keeps local neighbourhoods very well. That makes it a good tool for spotting mislabelled data: a '7' sitting inside the cluster of '1's is worth a look.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
emb = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit_transform(X)
print(emb.shape)                          # one 2D point per image

# How often is a point's nearest 2D neighbour the same digit?
d = ((emb[:, None, :] - emb[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
np.fill_diagonal(d, np.inf)
nn = d.argmin(axis=1)
print("same-digit nearest neighbour:", round((y[nn] == y).mean(), 3))
# To plot: plt.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=y, s=5)

# Output:
# (1797, 2)
# same-digit nearest neighbour: 0.988

# Storage arithmetic for stored embeddings (4 bytes per float32 number)
for dims in [1536, 512, 256]:
    gb = 1_000_000 * dims * 4 / 1e9
    print(f"1 million vectors x {dims:>4} dims = {gb:.1f} GB")

# Output (storage):
# 1 million vectors x 1536 dims = 6.1 GB
# 1 million vectors x  512 dims = 2.0 GB
# 1 million vectors x  256 dims = 1.0 GB

replace_subtopics.title: Kinds of anomalies
replace_subtopics.body:
Before choosing a method, name the kind of anomaly you are hunting. A point anomaly is one value that is odd on its own: a 9,000 euro coffee-shop payment. A contextual anomaly is a value that is normal in one context and odd in another: 290 logins is ordinary at noon and alarming at 3am. A collective anomaly is a group of points that is odd together even if each one looks fine: fifty 1 euro payments from one card in ten minutes, a classic card-testing pattern.

Then check what you have. How many columns? Is there a time order? Do you have any confirmed bad cases, and are they recent? Is there a clean stretch of normal data? The answers point to a method, as the table shows.

Finally, agree what happens to a flagged case. A fraud alert might block a payment, a monitoring alert might page an engineer, and a data-quality alert might just go in a report. The action decides how many false alarms are acceptable.

Turning context and groups into columns. Most tabular detectors, such as isolation forest, only see one row at a time. The usual trick is to build features that carry the context into the row. Velocity features count recent activity: payments by this card in the last 10 minutes, or logins from this IP address in the last hour. Aggregate features compare a value with the entity's own history: this amount divided by the card's median amount over the last 30 days. After that, a burst of tiny payments shows up as one row with a count of 50, and a normal-sized payment that is huge for this particular customer shows up as a ratio of 40. Collective and contextual anomalies have become point anomalies that any method in this lesson can score. Compute these features only from data before the current row, so live scoring and training see the same thing.
replace_subtopics.example: A payments startup, Orvella Payments (made up), asks for 'AI fraud detection'. In the first meeting the FDE sorts their worries into the three kinds: single huge refunds (point), card payments at unusual hours for that merchant (contextual) and bursts of tiny test payments (collective). Each gets a different detector, and the burst rule turns out to be a simple count per card per 10 minutes. For the contextual worry, the FDE adds a second feature, amount divided by the card's own 30-day median, so a 300 euro payment from a card that usually spends 8 euro stands out even though 300 euro is ordinary across all customers.

replace_subtopics.title: Z-scores and IQR fences
replace_subtopics.body:
The simplest detector asks how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean. That number is the z-score: z = (x - mean) / sd. With roughly bell-shaped data, |z| above 3 happens about 3 times in 1,000, so 3 is a common first threshold.

The z-score has a weakness called masking: big anomalies inflate the mean and standard deviation they are measured against, which hides smaller anomalies. The IQR method is more robust. Take the 25th percentile (Q1) and the 75th percentile (Q3); the interquartile range is IQR = Q3 - Q1. Tukey's fences flag anything below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR. Percentiles barely move when a few extreme values appear. A related robust option is the modified z-score. It swaps the mean for the median and the standard deviation for the median absolute deviation (MAD): take each value's distance from the median, then take the median of those distances. The formula is modified z = 0.6745 x (x - median) / MAD, and the usual threshold is |modified z| above 3.5. The 0.6745 rescales MAD so the number reads like an ordinary z-score on bell-shaped data. Because medians ignore a few extreme values, the big spike cannot hide the smaller one. One catch: if more than half the values are identical, MAD is 0 and the formula divides by zero, so fall back to IQR in that case.

Both methods look at one number at a time. They are ideal for a first pass, for data-quality checks and for explaining an alert in one sentence.
replace_subtopics.example: A café chain, Pembrook Cafés (made up), sees 12 to 16 refunds a day at one shop, then 95 on one day and 60 on another. The 95 inflates the standard deviation so much that the 60 gets a z-score of only 1.6 and is missed. The IQR fences (8.1 to 19.1) flag both days. The 60 turned out to be a staff member refunding cash sales to themselves. The modified z-score agrees with IQR: with a median of 14 and a MAD of 1.5, both spike days score far above 3.5.

import numpy as np

# Daily card refunds at one store (count per day); two suspicious days
refunds = np.array([12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 16, 12, 95, 14, 13, 15, 60, 12, 14])

z = (refunds - refunds.mean()) / refunds.std()
print("z-scores of spikes:", np.round(z[[7, 11]], 2))
print("flagged by |z| > 3:", np.where(np.abs(z) > 3)[0])

q1, q3 = np.percentile(refunds, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr    # Tukey fences
print(f"IQR fences: {low:.1f} to {high:.1f}")
print("flagged by IQR:", np.where((refunds < low) | (refunds > high))[0])

# Output:
# z-scores of spikes: [3.09 1.6 ]
# flagged by |z| > 3: [7]
# IQR fences: 8.1 to 19.1
# flagged by IQR: [ 7 11]

med = np.median(refunds)
mad = np.median(np.abs(refunds - med))          # median absolute deviation
mz = 0.6745 * (refunds - med) / mad              # modified z-score
print(f"median {med}, MAD {mad}")
print("modified z of spikes:", np.round(mz[[7, 11]], 1))
print("flagged by |modified z| > 3.5:", np.where(np.abs(mz) > 3.5)[0])

# Output (modified z-score):
# median 14.0, MAD 1.5
# modified z of spikes: [36.4 20.7]
# flagged by |modified z| > 3.5: [ 7 11]

replace_subtopics.title: One-class and novelty approaches
replace_subtopics.body:
Sometimes you have a clean sample of normal data only: a month of readings from a healthy pump, or logins from before an attack. One-class methods learn the boundary of that normal set and flag new points that fall outside it. This is called novelty detection. Outlier detection is the other case, where the training data itself may already contain anomalies.

Two common tools in scikit-learn. OneClassSVM draws a flexible boundary around the training data; its nu setting is roughly the share of training points allowed outside. LocalOutlierFactor (LOF) compares each point's local density with its neighbours' density; set novelty=True to score new points. Both use distances, so scale the columns first.

The risk is that 'normal' changes. If the pump is serviced or the product launches in a new country, yesterday's boundary flags everything. Plan to retrain on fresh normal data and watch the daily alert rate.

Reconstruction error is a third novelty approach, and the standard one for sensor data with many related columns. Train a model that squeezes each healthy row into a few numbers and then rebuilds it: PCA with a few components (see dimred), or a small neural network called an autoencoder that does the same with curves. On healthy data the sensors move together (more load means more current, more heat, more vibration), so the rebuild is close. A faulty row breaks that pattern and cannot be rebuilt well, so the gap between the row and its rebuild, the reconstruction error, is large. Set the alert threshold from the errors on held-back healthy data, for example their 99th percentile. A bonus: the per-column error shows which sensor broke the pattern, which helps the engineer.
replace_subtopics.example: A water utility, Kestrelford Water (made up), trains on 500 hourly readings from a healthy pump: temperature around 60 C and vibration around 3 mm/s. Four new readings arrive. Both methods pass the first two and flag the third (vibration 5.5, a worn bearing) and the fourth (75 C, a blocked cooling line), without a single labelled failure.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
# Sensor readings (temperature C, vibration mm/s) from a healthy pump only
healthy = np.column_stack([rng.normal(60, 2, 500), rng.normal(3, 0.4, 500)])
new = np.array([[61, 3.1], [59, 2.8], [62, 5.5], [75, 3.0]])   # last two look wrong

ocsvm = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), OneClassSVM(nu=0.01, gamma="scale")).fit(healthy)
print("one-class SVM:", ocsvm.predict(new))     # 1 = like training data, -1 = novel

lof = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, novelty=True)).fit(healthy)
print("LOF novelty:  ", lof.predict(new))

# Output:
# one-class SVM: [ 1  1 -1 -1]
# LOF novelty:   [ 1  1 -1 -1]

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

# Reconstruction error: three sensors that all rise with pump load
load = rng.uniform(0.3, 1.0, 500)
healthy3 = np.column_stack([40 + 30 * load, 5 + 10 * load, 1 + 3 * load]) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, (500, 3))
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(healthy3)
pca = PCA(n_components=1).fit(scaler.transform(healthy3))   # one "load" direction

def recon_error(rows):
    z = scaler.transform(rows)
    return np.linalg.norm(z - pca.inverse_transform(pca.transform(z)), axis=1)

threshold = np.percentile(recon_error(healthy3), 99)
# temperature, current, vibration: a normal row, then high current at low temperature
new3 = np.array([[61, 12.0, 3.1], [50, 14.0, 2.2]])
print(f"threshold {threshold:.2f}, errors {np.round(recon_error(new3), 2)}")
print("flagged:", recon_error(new3) > threshold)

# Output (reconstruction error):
# threshold 0.94, errors [0.   2.12]
# flagged: [False  True]

replace_subtopics.title: Time-based anomalies
replace_subtopics.body:
Time series add context. 290 logins is normal at noon and alarming at 3am. A global z-score over all hours misses both kinds of problem, because the daily cycle itself makes the standard deviation large.

The fix is to compare each point with a baseline for its own context: the same hour of day, the same weekday, or a forecast. Compute the residual (actual minus expected) and score the residual instead of the raw value. Simple versions use the median of the same hour over recent weeks; stronger versions use a forecasting model (see timeseries) and flag points outside its prediction interval.

Also decide what counts as one incident. A 40-minute outage produces 40 anomalous minutes, so group consecutive flags into a single alert and add a short cool-down, so the on-call engineer gets one page, not forty.

Not every problem is a spike. A level shift is when the line jumps to a new level and stays there, for example error rate moving from 2 to 2.35 percent after a release. Drift is a slow creep, such as a sensor losing calibration a little each day. No single point looks odd, so point detectors stay silent. Change-point detection looks for the moment the average moved. The simple version compares a short recent window with a longer earlier one: if the last 7 days' mean sits several standard errors away from the previous 28 days' mean, raise an alert. A classic method is CUSUM (cumulative sum): add up each day's excess over the expected level, minus a small allowance, and alarm when the running total passes a limit. Small daily excesses that are each harmless add up quickly, so CUSUM catches small persistent shifts that a z-score never would.
replace_subtopics.example: A software company monitors hourly logins over two weeks, with a strong daily cycle. Two problems are injected: an extra 150 logins at a busy noon, and 290 logins at 3am when about 100 is normal. A global z-score flags nothing. A same-hour baseline flags both, and the 3am burst turns out to be a credential-stuffing attack (someone trying stolen passwords).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
idx = pd.date_range("2026-05-01", periods=24 * 14, freq="h")      # two weeks, hourly
hour = idx.hour.to_numpy()
logins = 200 + 150 * np.sin((hour - 6) / 24 * 2 * np.pi) + rng.normal(0, 15, len(idx))
s = pd.Series(logins, index=idx)
s.iloc[300] = s.iloc[300] + 150        # a spike, but at a busy hour
s.iloc[315] = 290                      # 3am: normal for noon, odd for night

glob_z = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()      # global z-score ignores the daily cycle
same_hour = s.groupby(s.index.hour)
ctx_z = (s - same_hour.transform("median")) / same_hour.transform("std")
print("global |z|>3 flags:", list(s.index[glob_z.abs() > 3].strftime("%d %H:00")))
print("same-hour |z|>3 flags:", list(s.index[ctx_z.abs() > 3].strftime("%d %H:00")))

# Output:
# global |z|>3 flags: []
# same-hour |z|>3 flags: ['13 12:00', '14 03:00']

# A level shift: daily error rate moves from about 2.0 to 2.35 percent on day 40
days = pd.date_range("2026-03-01", periods=70, freq="D")
err = pd.Series(np.r_[rng.normal(2.0, 0.25, 40), rng.normal(2.35, 0.25, 30)], index=days)
z = (err - err[:30].mean()) / err[:30].std()
print("days with |z| > 3:", int((z.abs() > 3).sum()))      # no clear spike to point at

# CUSUM: add up excess over the old level, minus an allowance k; alarm above limit h
target, sd = err[:30].mean(), err[:30].std()
k, h, total = 0.5 * sd, 5 * sd, 0.0
for day, x in err.items():
    total = max(0.0, total + (x - target - k))
    if total > h:
        print("CUSUM alarm on", day.strftime("%d %b"), "(shift started 10 Apr)")
        break

# Output (level shift):
# days with |z| > 3: 0
# CUSUM alarm on 15 Apr (shift started 10 Apr)

add_glossary: Modified z-score
A robust z-score: 0.6745 x (x - median) / MAD, usually flagged above 3.5.
MAD
Median absolute deviation: the median of each value's distance from the median.
Reconstruction error

add_subtopics.title: Prediction intervals and quantile forecasts
add_subtopics.body:
A forecast of 150 loaves is really a guess that could land anywhere from 140 to 160. The decision often depends on that spread, not on the middle. A bakery that runs out loses sales and annoys customers, so it may want to bake enough to cover 9 days out of 10. A call centre plans staff for a busy but plausible day, not an average one. That is why good forecasts come with a prediction interval: a range that should contain the actual value a stated share of the time, such as 80 percent.

There are two common ways to get one. Statistical models such as ARIMA and ETS estimate the size of their own errors, so statsmodels can return a range: get_forecast(h).conf_int(alpha=0.2) gives an 80 percent band (alpha is the share allowed outside). Tree models give a single number by default, but you can train them with quantile loss (also called pinball loss), which aims at a chosen percentile instead of the average. A P90 forecast is the value the actual should stay below 90 percent of the time. HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", quantile=0.9) and LightGBM's objective="quantile" both do this; train one model per percentile you need, such as P10, P50 and P90.

Intervals must be checked like point forecasts. In the backtest, count how often the actual falls inside the band. An 80 percent interval should cover roughly 80 percent of test points. Much less means the model is overconfident; much more means the band is too wide to be useful. Coverage on 14 test days is noisy, so judge it across all folds.
add_subtopics.example: Hartwell Bakeries (made up) wants to know how much to bake so it rarely runs out. The SARIMA model's 80 percent band for the first test day runs from 139 to 154 loaves. Only 64 percent of the 14 test days fall inside it, below the promised 80 percent, a hint that the band is a little too narrow, so the FDE checks coverage across all backtest folds before trusting it. A P90 boosting model is also trained, and 96 percent of test days land at or below it, so it is safe but a little generous. The FDE recommends baking to the P90 number for bread that keeps a day and to the P50 for cakes that go to waste, and puts both lines on one chart for the owner.
