import warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = pd.date_range("2025-01-06", periods=168, freq="D")
sales = pd.Series(100 + 0.3 * np.arange(168)
                  + np.array([0, 5, 8, 10, 25, 40, -20])[idx.dayofweek]
                  + rng.normal(0, 6, 168), index=idx).round()
train, test = sales[:-14], sales[-14:]

# 1) Statistical model: ask for a forecast distribution, not just a point
model = ARIMA(train, order=(1, 0, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7), trend="t").fit()
fc = model.get_forecast(14)
band = fc.conf_int(alpha=0.2)                    # 80% interval: 10th to 90th percentile
print(band.head(2).round().astype(int).to_string())
inside = ((test >= band.iloc[:, 0]) & (test <= band.iloc[:, 1])).mean()
print(f"SARIMA 80% interval coverage on the test: {inside:.0%}")

# 2) Machine learning: quantile loss trains a model for one chosen percentile
df = pd.DataFrame({"y": sales, "lag_7": sales.shift(7), "lag_14": sales.shift(14),
                   "dow": sales.index.dayofweek}).dropna()
tr, te = df.iloc[:-28], df.iloc[-28:]
X = ["lag_7", "lag_14", "dow"]
p90 = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", quantile=0.9, random_state=0)
p90.fit(tr[X], tr["y"] - tr["lag_7"])
high = te["lag_7"] + p90.predict(te[X])
print(f"share of test days at or below the P90 forecast: {(te['y'] <= high).mean():.0%}")

# Output:
#             lower y  upper y
# 2025-06-09      139      154
# 2025-06-10      143      158
# SARIMA 80% interval coverage on the test: 64%
# share of test days at or below the P90 forecast: 96%

add_subtopics.title: Preparing time data
add_subtopics.body:
Real data rarely arrives as a neat row per day. It comes as events (each sale, each login) with timestamps, and the first job is to build a regular grid: one row per hour, day or week. In pandas, resample("D").sum() turns events into daily totals and fills days with no events. asfreq("D") does the same for a series that already has one value per step but skips some.

Then decide what a gap means. A day with no sales in the data can be a real zero (the shop was open and sold nothing) or missing (the shop was closed, the till was offline, the file did not arrive). Filling a closed day with 0 teaches the model that demand dropped. Mark those days as missing, drop them from training or fill them from a similar day, and ask the customer which it is.

Time zones catch almost everyone. Systems often log in UTC, but the business thinks in local days. Convert to local time before grouping by day, or late-evening sales land on the next day. Daylight saving time makes one day a year 23 hours long and one 25 hours, which matters for hourly data.

Forecast at the level where the decision is made. If orders go to the supplier weekly per shop, forecast weekly per shop; forecasting each product by the hour adds noise nobody uses. Finally, collect a holiday and event calendar (public holidays, promotions, closures) and add it as feature columns. The customer usually has this list somewhere and it explains many of the biggest misses.
add_subtopics.example: Tillmoor Grocers (made up) sends a year of till events in UTC. After converting to London time and resampling to days (a few late-evening orders had been landing on the wrong day in UTC), the FDE finds 9 days with no rows. Asking the store manager shows 2 were real zero days and 7 were a broken till upload. Filling all 9 with 0 would have pulled the average down; instead the 7 are marked missing, and a holiday flag explains the three biggest spikes.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Raw web orders for a bakery: timestamps in UTC, only days with an order appear
events = pd.DataFrame({
    "ts": pd.to_datetime(["2026-03-28 09:15", "2026-03-28 17:40", "2026-03-29 23:30",
                          "2026-03-30 08:05", "2026-04-01 10:00", "2026-04-03 11:00"], utc=True),
    "loaves": [3, 5, 4, 2, 6, 9],
})
# 1) Group by LOCAL day. London moved to summer time on 29 March, so 23:30 UTC is 00:30 next day
utc_days = events.set_index("ts")["loaves"].resample("D").sum()
local = events.set_index(events["ts"].dt.tz_convert("Europe/London"))["loaves"]

                   index=daily.index).to_string())

# 2) A day with no orders is not always zero: the shop was closed for a refit on 31 March
daily.loc[pd.Timestamp("2026-03-31").date()] = np.nan    # unknown, not 'sold nothing'

print("mean skipping the closed day:  ", round(daily.mean(), 2))

# 3) Holiday flag as a feature (Good Friday 2026 is 3 April)
holidays = pd.to_datetime(["2026-04-03", "2026-04-06"]).date
print("is_holiday:", [int(d in holidays) for d in daily.index])

replace_subtopics.title: ARIMA at a high level
replace_subtopics.body:
ARIMA is a classic family of statistical models, and its name lists its three parts. AR (autoregressive, order p): today depends on the last p values. I (integrated, order d): difference the series d times (today minus yesterday) to remove trend, so its average stays stable. MA (moving average, order q): today depends on the last q forecast errors. This MA is about past errors, which is different from the moving average in the previous section.

Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA) adds the same three parts at the seasonal lag, written (P, D, Q, s), with s = 7 for a weekly pattern in daily data. Choosing orders used to be an art with ACF and PACF plots; today people usually try a few small orders and compare them with AIC (lower is better) and, more importantly, with a backtest.

The practical view for an FDE: ARIMA and ETS are well understood, fast and good on a single series with a few years of history. They get awkward with thousands of series, many outside drivers (price, weather, promotions) or messy data, which is where the next section comes in.

Stationarity in one line: a series is stationary when its average and spread do not change over time, with no trend and no changing season. ARIMA's AR and MA parts assume stationarity, which is why the I part differences the series first. The standard check is the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test: its p-value asks 'could this series have a unit root, that is, wander without returning to a fixed level?'. A p-value below 0.05 suggests the series is stationary; above 0.05, difference it and test again. This question comes up in almost every forecasting interview.
replace_subtopics.example: A seasonal ARIMA with order (1, 0, 1), a weekly seasonal part (0, 1, 1, 7) and a trend term gets MAE 4.8 on the bakery holdout, very close to Holt-Winters at 4.9. When two sensible models agree this closely, pick the one the customer's team can maintain and explain.

replace_subtopics.title: Gradient boosting with lag features
replace_subtopics.body:
You can turn forecasting into ordinary supervised learning (see boosting). Each row is a day, the target is that day's value, and the features are things known before that day: lag features (the value 1, 7 or 14 days earlier), rolling averages of past values, the day of the week, holidays and planned promotions.

Three details matter. Every feature must exist at forecast time: if you forecast 14 days ahead, yesterday's value does not exist yet, so use only lags of at least the horizon, or forecast one step at a time. Shift before rolling, so a rolling mean never includes the target day. And tree models cannot extrapolate: they never predict above the highest value seen in training, so with a rising trend predict the change from last week and add it back.

The big win is scale and outside drivers. One model can learn from thousands of shops or products at once, with price, weather and promotions as features, which classic single-series models find hard.

Other tools a customer may already use. Prophet (from Meta) fits trend, seasons and holidays with little setup and is common in analytics teams; it is easy to use but often loses to a tuned ETS or boosting model in backtests. statsforecast from Nixtla runs ETS, ARIMA and Croston very fast across thousands of series, and its sister library mlforecast builds lag features for boosting for you. Pretrained time-series foundation models, such as Amazon's Chronos and Google's TimesFM, were trained on huge numbers of series and can forecast a new one with no training at all (zero-shot). Treat every one of these the same way: run it through the same backtest, next to seasonal naive, and keep it only if it wins on the metric the customer cares about.
replace_subtopics.example: Forecasting tomorrow's bakery sales each night over the last 28 days: boosting that predicts sales directly scores MAE 6.1, slightly worse than seasonal naive at 6.0, because the trees cannot follow the upward trend. Predicting the change versus last week instead scores 5.7. The gain is small because this synthetic series has no promotions or weather; on real data, those extra features are where boosting pulls ahead.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = pd.date_range("2025-01-06", periods=168, freq="D")
sales = pd.Series(100 + 0.3 * np.arange(168)
                  + np.array([0, 5, 8, 10, 25, 40, -20])[idx.dayofweek]
                  + rng.normal(0, 6, 168), index=idx).round()

# Task: each night, forecast tomorrow. So any value up to today is allowed.
df = pd.DataFrame({"y": sales})
df["lag_1"] = df["y"].shift(1)            # yesterday
df["lag_7"] = df["y"].shift(7)            # same weekday last week
df["lag_14"] = df["y"].shift(14)
df["lag_21"] = df["y"].shift(21)
df["mean_7"] = df["y"].shift(1).rolling(7).mean()   # shift(1) first: never include the target day
df["dow"] = df.index.dayofweek
df = df.dropna()

train, test = df.iloc[:-28], df.iloc[-28:]    # split by time, never shuffle
X_cols = ["lag_1", "lag_7", "lag_14", "lag_21", "mean_7", "dow"]
gbm = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)
for target in ["level", "change"]:
    if target == "level":                     # predict sales directly
        gbm.fit(train[X_cols], train["y"])
        pred = gbm.predict(test[X_cols])
    else:                                     # predict change vs last week, then add it back
        gbm.fit(train[X_cols], train["y"] - train["lag_7"])
        pred = test["lag_7"] + gbm.predict(test[X_cols])
    print(f"boosting ({target}) MAE:", round(np.abs(test["y"] - pred).mean(), 1))
print("seasonal naive MAE:", round(np.abs(test["y"] - test["lag_7"]).mean(), 1))

# Output:
# boosting (level) MAE: 6.1
# boosting (change) MAE: 5.7
# seasonal naive MAE: 6.0

replace_subtopics.title: Backtesting and the MAPE trap
replace_subtopics.body:
A random train/test split leaks the future into training. For time series, always split by time. A backtest (also called time-series cross-validation or rolling-origin evaluation) repeats this several times: train up to a cut-off, forecast the next h periods, score, move the cut-off forward and repeat. Averaging over folds shows whether a model is reliably better or got lucky in one period. scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit produces these folds.

Choose the error metric with care. MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) is popular because '8 percent off' sounds clear, but it divides by the actual value. One zero-sales day makes it infinite, low-volume items dominate the average, and it punishes over-forecasts more than under-forecasts, which quietly rewards forecasting too low. Safer choices: MAE in units; WAPE, the sum of absolute errors divided by the sum of actuals; or MASE, the error divided by the seasonal-naive error, so below 1 means you beat the baseline.

Finally, agree with the customer on the horizon (next day or next month?) and the level (per shop, per product, or total). An accuracy number means nothing without both.

Intermittent demand is its own case: a spare part or a slow product that sells 0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, 2 and so on. Seasonal naive and ETS behave badly here, and MAPE is useless because of the zeros. Croston's method splits the series into two smaller problems: how big a sale is when it happens, and how many periods pass between sales. It smooths each one and forecasts their ratio, a steady average demand per period (variants such as SBA correct a small bias). Score these series only with WAPE or MASE. In the example code Croston's MASE of 0.69 beats the naive error, while its WAPE above 1 shows how hard such a series is to forecast week by week, which is why stock decisions for rare items usually use the total over the lead time. Remember too that a forecast of all zeros can look accurate on MAE while being useless for stocking, so check the total too.
replace_subtopics.example: Four folds of 14 days each give seasonal-naive MAE of 8.6, 8.1, 6.1 and 5.4. That spread shows how much results vary by period, so a model that beat the baseline only in the last fold proves little. For a slow-selling product with a zero day, MAPE comes out infinite, while WAPE gives a sensible 9 percent.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = pd.date_range("2025-01-06", periods=168, freq="D")
y = pd.Series(100 + 0.3 * np.arange(168)
              + np.array([0, 5, 8, 10, 25, 40, -20])[idx.dayofweek]
              + rng.normal(0, 6, 168), index=idx).round().to_numpy()

tss = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=4, test_size=14)       # each fold: train on the past, test on next 14 days
for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(tss.split(y)):
    fc = y[tr][-7:][np.arange(len(te)) % 7]           # seasonal naive from the end of the train window
    print(f"fold {i}: train up to day {tr[-1]}, MAE {np.abs(y[te] - fc).mean():.1f}")

actual = np.array([0, 2, 50, 48])                     # a slow product with a zero day
pred = np.array([1, 1, 45, 50])
with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
    print("MAPE:", np.mean(np.abs(actual - pred) / actual))      # inf because of the zero
print("WAPE:", round(np.abs(actual - pred).sum() / actual.sum(), 3))

# Output:
# fold 0: train up to day 111, MAE 8.6
# fold 1: train up to day 125, MAE 8.1
# fold 2: train up to day 139, MAE 6.1
# fold 3: train up to day 153, MAE 5.4
# MAPE: inf
# WAPE: 0.09

# Intermittent demand: a spare part that sells rarely
demand = np.array([0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 2])

def croston(y, alpha=0.1):
    size, gap, periods = None, None, 1
    for v in y:
        if v > 0:
            size = v if size is None else alpha * v + (1 - alpha) * size
            gap = periods if gap is None else alpha * periods + (1 - alpha) * gap
            periods = 1
        else:
            periods += 1
    return size / gap                               # average demand per period

train_d, test_d = demand[:16], demand[16:]
fc = croston(train_d)
print(f"Croston forecast per week: {fc:.2f}")
wape = np.abs(test_d - fc).sum() / test_d.sum()
naive_mae = np.abs(np.diff(train_d)).mean()         # in-sample naive error, the MASE scale
mase = np.abs(test_d - fc).mean() / naive_mae
print(f"WAPE {wape:.2f}, MASE {mase:.2f}")

# Output (intermittent demand):
# Croston forecast per week: 0.92
# WAPE 1.26, MASE 0.69
checklist: Split by time and never shuffle
Backtest over at least 3 to 5 folds
Match the test horizon to how the forecast will be used
Report the baseline error next to the model error
Use MAE, WAPE or MASE; avoid MAPE when zeros or tiny values occur
Check every feature exists at forecast time
Note holidays and one-off events that explain big misses
For intermittent demand, try Croston and score only with WAPE or MASE

add_glossary: Prediction interval
A range that should contain the future actual value a stated share of the time, such as 80 percent.
Quantile forecast
A forecast for a chosen percentile, such as P90: the actual should be below it 90 percent of the time.
Quantile loss
A training loss, also called pinball loss, that makes a model aim at a chosen percentile instead of the average.
Interval coverage
The share of test points that fall inside the prediction interval; it should match the promised level.
Resample
Turning events or irregular data into a regular grid, such as one total per day.
Stationary
A series whose average and spread do not change over time.
ADF test
Augmented Dickey-Fuller test; a p-value below 0.05 suggests the series is stationary.
Intermittent demand
A series with many zero periods, such as a slow spare part.
Croston's method
A forecast for intermittent demand that smooths sale size and the gap between sales separately.
MASE
Mean absolute scaled error: model error divided by a naive forecast's error; below 1 beats the baseline.
Foundation model (time series)
A model pretrained on many series, such as Chronos or TimesFM, that can forecast a new series without training.

add_subtopics.title: Two-stage production architecture
add_subtopics.body:
A shop with a million products cannot run a careful model on every product for every page view. Production recommenders therefore work in stages, the pattern the animation on this page shows.

Stage 1, candidate retrieval, is fast and rough. It pulls a few hundred items from several sources and merges them. Co-visitation counts record how often two items appear in the same session or basket; they are just counts, updated nightly, and are surprisingly strong. Embedding retrieval gives every item a vector (from matrix factorization, a text embedding model or a two-tower model) and uses approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) search to find items near the user's vector in milliseconds (see embeddings and rag). A two-tower model is a neural network with one tower that turns a user into a vector and another that turns an item into a vector, trained so that the dot product is high for items the user engaged with. Popularity per segment and fresh items are other common sources.

Stage 2, ranking, is slow and careful but only sees those few hundred candidates. A learning-to-rank model, often LightGBM's LGBMRanker, scores each candidate with many features: user history, item price and stock, co-visit counts, time of day, device. It is trained on impression logs, with bought or clicked items as the positives.

Stage 3 applies business rules: remove owned and out-of-stock items, respect age limits, cap how many items from one brand appear, pin a promotion. Finally, decide the serving mode. Precomputed lists (built nightly per user and cached) are cheap and simple; real-time scoring reacts to what the user did a minute ago but needs a low-latency service. Many teams precompute candidates and rank in real time.
add_subtopics.example: Brackenfield Outdoor (made up) sells 80,000 items. Nightly co-visitation counts show that after a tent, shoppers most often also viewed a stove (3 sessions), a lamp and a mat. These plus 200 embedding neighbours and 50 popular items form each user's candidates. A LightGBM ranker using co-visit count, popularity and price gap lifts NDCG@5 from 0.58 (sorting by co-visits alone) to 0.76 on held-out users. A rule then removes out-of-stock items before the top 10 are shown.
add_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter
from itertools import permutations
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.metrics import ndcg_score

# Stage 1: co-visitation candidates from browsing sessions
sessions = [["tent", "stove", "lamp"], ["tent", "mat", "stove"], ["stove", "gas", "pan"],
            ["tent", "lamp", "mat"], ["kettle", "mugs"], ["tent", "stove", "gas"]]
covisit = Counter()
for s in sessions:
    for a, b in permutations(set(s), 2):
        covisit[(a, b)] += 1                    # a and b seen in the same session
cands = sorted(((b, n) for (a, b), n in covisit.items() if a == "tent"), key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0]))
print("candidates after 'tent':", cands)

# Stage 2: a learning-to-rank model on candidate features
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_users, n_cands = 400, 20
covis = rng.poisson(3, (n_users, n_cands)).astype(float)   # co-visit count with user's last item
pop = rng.random((n_users, n_cands))                        # item popularity, 0..1
price_gap = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_users, n_cands))            # price vs what the user usually pays
X = np.stack([covis, pop, price_gap], axis=-1)
true = 0.5 * covis + 2 * pop - 1.5 * np.abs(price_gap) + rng.normal(0, 1, (n_users, n_cands))
rel = np.digitize(true, np.quantile(true, [0.7, 0.9]))      # 0, 1 or 2 = bought
tr, te = slice(0, 300), slice(300, 400)
ranker = lgb.LGBMRanker(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=-1, random_state=0)

replace_subtopics.title: Content-based recommendations
replace_subtopics.body:
Content-based methods recommend items similar to ones the user liked, using the items' own attributes: text descriptions, categories, brand, price band, or embeddings of product text and images. Each item becomes a vector, and similarity is usually cosine similarity, the angle between two vectors, where 1 means the same direction and 0 means unrelated.

TF-IDF is a simple way to turn text into vectors: words that are frequent in one description but rare across the catalogue get more weight. A modern alternative is to embed each description with a text embedding model (see embeddings) and compare those vectors.

Strengths: it works for a brand-new item the moment it has a description, and every suggestion is easy to explain ('because you viewed Trail runner 2'). Weaknesses: it recommends more of the same and rarely surprises, and it is only as good as the catalogue data.

Large language models help in two places. First, thin catalogues: many shops have items with a title and nothing else, which gives content-based methods nothing to work with. An LLM can write a short, consistent description and a fixed set of tags (activity, season, material, style) for every item from its title, supplier sheet or photo, and those fields feed TF-IDF or an embedding model. Give the model a fixed tag list to choose from, check a sample by hand, and never let it invent facts such as sizes or safety ratings. Second, explanations: given the item the user bought and the recommended item, an LLM can write one plain sentence such as 'Because you bought a trail shoe: these socks are made for the same muddy runs'. Generate these offline for the most common pairs to keep costs and latency low.
replace_subtopics.example: At an outdoor shop, a user views 'Trail runner 2'. TF-IDF over five product descriptions ranks 'Road racer' first (similarity 0.40, sharing lightweight, running and shoe), then 'Running socks' (0.26), then 'Hiking boot' (0.14, sharing mud). The rain jacket shares no words and is not suggested. The shop's new 'Merino trail sock' has only a title, so it would never be matched. An LLM writes a description with the tags running, trail and lightweight, and the sock now appears next to the trail shoe with a one-line reason.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

items = {
    "Trail runner 2":   "lightweight trail running shoe grip mud",
    "Road racer":       "lightweight road running shoe racing",
    "Hiking boot":      "waterproof hiking boot ankle support mud",
    "Rain jacket":      "waterproof jacket hiking rain",
    "Running socks":    "running socks lightweight blister",
}

replace_subtopics.title: Implicit feedback and cold start
replace_subtopics.body:
Explicit feedback is a user stating a preference: a star rating or a thumbs up. It is clear but rare. Implicit feedback is behaviour: views, clicks, add-to-cart, purchases, minutes watched. It is plentiful but noisy. A missing interaction may mean 'not interested' or simply 'never saw it', and a click may be a mis-tap. Most business data is implicit, so treat it as a confidence signal (a purchase counts more than a view) and never treat unseen items as dislikes.

Cold start is the problem of new users and new items with no history. For new users, start with popularity for their region or entry page, ask two or three onboarding questions, or use what they have done in this session. For new items, lean on content-based similarity until they collect interactions, and reserve a small share of slots for fresh items so they get seen.

Most production systems are hybrids: they combine popularity, content and CF signals, and a ranking model decides the final order.

Position bias is the other trap in implicit data. Items shown at the top of a list get more clicks just because they are at the top: people scan from the top and stop early. If you train on raw clicks, the model learns 'whatever we ranked first is good' and keeps ranking it first. The fix starts with logging: for every impression, record the item, the position it was shown in and whether it was clicked. Then compare items fairly, for example by dividing each click-through rate by the average click-through rate for that position, as the code does: raw click rate says the tent is best, but once each click is compared with what its slot usually earns, the lamp, which was mostly shown at the bottom, comes out on top. Another fix is to add position as a feature during training and set it to the same value for every item when scoring.
replace_subtopics.example: An online grocer, Tamberlin Fresh (made up), adds 300 new products a month. Pure CF never recommends them, because nobody has bought them yet, so they never get bought. The FDE adds a content-based candidate source for items under 30 days old and reserves 1 of every 10 slots for them. New products start collecting purchases within a week and move into the CF model naturally.

import pandas as pd

replace_subtopics.title: Offline metrics and A/B testing
replace_subtopics.body:
To evaluate offline, hide each user's most recent interactions, recommend from their older history, and check how many hidden items appear in the top k. Precision@k is hits divided by k. Recall@k is hits divided by the number of hidden items. NDCG@k (normalised discounted cumulative gain) also rewards putting hits near the top: a hit at position i counts 1 / log2(i + 1), and the total is divided by the best possible score, so 1.0 is perfect.

Split by time, as in forecasting: train on events before a date and test on events after it, or the model learns from the future. Also check coverage (what share of the catalogue ever gets recommended), so you do not just rebuild the bestseller list.

Offline metrics suggest value but do not prove it. The real test is an A/B test (see stats): randomly send some users to the new recommender and some to the old one, agree the primary metric in advance (for example revenue per session or add-to-cart rate), run for whole weeks to cover weekly cycles, and check guardrail metrics such as returns and page speed.

Accuracy is not the only goal. Diversity asks whether one list mixes different kinds of items or shows five nearly identical tents. Novelty asks whether the list includes less obvious items the user was unlikely to find alone; a common measure is the average of -log2(item popularity share), which is higher for rarer items. Popularity bias is the tendency of most recommenders to push already-popular items, so check what share of recommendations comes from the top 10 percent of items.

These matter because of feedback loops. A recommender only learns from what it showed: items it never shows collect no clicks, look bad in the next training run and are shown even less. To break the loop, reserve a small exploration share, for example 5 percent of slots, for items chosen at random or from under-shown candidates, and log them so their results can be used as fairer training data.
replace_subtopics.example: A user's held-out week contains a tent and a stove. Model A recommends them in positions 1 and 2; model B in positions 4 and 5. Both have precision@5 of 0.40 and recall@5 of 1.00, but NDCG@5 is 1.00 for A and 0.50 for B, because few users scroll to position 5. NDCG captures the difference that precision misses. Looking only at the top 3, model A (tent, stove, lamp) mixes camping and cooking items, while model B (lamp, mat, chair) is all camping but made of rarer items, so it scores lower on diversity and higher on novelty. Which matters more is a business choice to agree with the customer.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

def precision_recall_at_k(recs, relevant, k):
    hits = len(set(recs[:k]) & relevant)
    return hits / k, hits / len(relevant)

def ndcg_at_k(recs, relevant, k):
    dcg = sum(1 / np.log2(i + 2) for i, r in enumerate(recs[:k]) if r in relevant)
    ideal = sum(1 / np.log2(i + 2) for i in range(min(k, len(relevant))))
    return dcg / ideal                      # 1.0 = hits all at the very top

relevant = {"tent", "stove"}               # what the user bought in the held-out week
model_a = ["tent", "stove", "lamp", "mat", "chair"]
model_b = ["lamp", "mat", "chair", "tent", "stove"]
for name, recs in [("A", model_a), ("B", model_b)]:
    p, r = precision_recall_at_k(recs, relevant, 5)
    print(f"model {name}: precision@5 {p:.2f}, recall@5 {r:.2f}, NDCG@5 {ndcg_at_k(recs, relevant, 5):.2f}")

# Output:
# model A: precision@5 0.40, recall@5 1.00, NDCG@5 1.00
# model B: precision@5 0.40, recall@5 1.00, NDCG@5 0.50

# Diversity and novelty for the same two lists
category = {"tent": "camp", "stove": "cook", "lamp": "camp", "mat": "camp", "chair": "camp"}
share = {"tent": 0.30, "stove": 0.25, "lamp": 0.05, "mat": 0.02, "chair": 0.01}   # popularity share

def diversity(recs):                       # share of item pairs from different categories
    pairs = [(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(recs) for b in recs[i + 1:]]
    return np.mean([category[a] != category[b] for a, b in pairs])

def novelty(recs):                         # rarer items give higher scores
    return np.mean([-np.log2(share[r]) for r in recs])

for name, recs in [("A", model_a[:3]), ("B", model_b[:3])]:
    print(f"model {name} top 3 {recs}: diversity {diversity(recs):.2f}, novelty {novelty(recs):.1f}")

# Output (beyond accuracy):
# model A top 3 ['tent', 'stove', 'lamp']: diversity 0.67, novelty 2.7
# model B top 3 ['lamp', 'mat', 'chair']: diversity 0.00, novelty 5.5

add_subtopics.title: Many classes and a real PyTorch training loop
add_subtopics.body:
So far the network gave one probability for a yes or no question. Most real tasks have many classes: which of ten digits is in the picture, which of six queues a ticket belongs to. The change is small. The output layer has one raw score per class (these raw scores are called logits), and softmax turns them into probabilities that add up to 1. The loss is then cross-entropy for many classes: minus the log of the probability given to the correct class.

In PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects the raw logits and the correct class number (0, 1, 2 ...), not probabilities and not one-hot vectors. It applies softmax inside, in a numerically safe way. A very common beginner bug is to add a softmax layer at the end of the model and then use CrossEntropyLoss, which squashes the scores twice and slows learning. Apply softmax yourself only when you want to read the probabilities.

Real data does not fit in memory as one block, so you wrap it in a Dataset and let a DataLoader hand out shuffled batches. The loop has the same shape every time: for each batch, clear old gradients with opt.zero_grad(), run the forward pass, compute the loss, call loss.backward(), and step the optimizer. After each epoch you switch to model.eval() and torch.no_grad() and measure loss and accuracy on the validation set. Move model and batches to a GPU with .to(device) when one exists; the code still runs on a CPU, only slower. Finally, save model.state_dict(), the learned numbers only, and load it into a model built the same way.
add_subtopics.example: A support team at Larkfield Telecom sorts tickets into ten queues. The model outputs ten logits, CrossEntropyLoss compares them with the true queue number, and after 15 epochs of batches of 64 the validation accuracy is about 94 percent. The team saves the state_dict, and the web service rebuilds the same layers and loads it. The digits data below stands in for tickets so the whole example runs in seconds.
add_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

torch.manual_seed(0)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"     # use a GPU when there is one

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)                          # 1,797 images, 10 classes (0-9)
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X / 16.0, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
to_ds = lambda a, b: TensorDataset(torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(b))
train_dl = DataLoader(to_ds(X_tr, y_tr), batch_size=64, shuffle=True)   # batches of 64
val_dl = DataLoader(to_ds(X_val, y_val), batch_size=256)

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10)).to(device)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()              # takes RAW scores (logits); softmax is inside
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for epoch in range(1, 16):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in train_dl:
        xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    model.eval()
    correct, val_loss = 0, 0.0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for xb, yb in val_dl:
            xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
            logits = model(xb)
            val_loss += loss_fn(logits, yb).item() * len(yb)
            correct += (logits.argmax(1) == yb).sum().item()
    if epoch % 5 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}  val loss {val_loss / len(y_val):.3f}  val accuracy {correct / len(y_val):.3f}")

probs = torch.softmax(model(val_dl.dataset[:1][0].to(device)), dim=1)   # softmax only to read probabilities
print("first validation image: predicted", probs.argmax(1).item(), "true", y_val[0],
      "confidence", round(probs.max().item(), 3))
torch.save(model.state_dict(), "digits_model.pt")            # save the weights, not the whole object
model2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
model2.load_state_dict(torch.load("digits_model.pt", map_location="cpu"))
print("reloaded weights OK")

# Output (CPU run, seed 0; numbers can differ slightly on another machine):
# epoch  5  val loss 1.097  val accuracy 0.872
# epoch 10  val loss 0.468  val accuracy 0.936
# epoch 15  val loss 0.292  val accuracy 0.942
# first validation image: predicted 2 true 2 confidence 0.96
# reloaded weights OK

replace_subtopics.title: Activation functions
replace_subtopics.body:
An activation function is the small bend applied after the weighted sum. It matters because a stack of layers with no bend is mathematically the same as one layer: multiplying by one grid of weights and then another is still just multiplying by a single combined grid. The bend is what lets a deep network draw curved boundaries.

The classic choices are sigmoid, which squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, and tanh, which squashes into -1 to 1. Both flatten out for large inputs, so their slope is almost zero there and learning slows. ReLU (rectified linear unit) simply turns negatives into zero and keeps positives. It is cheap and does not flatten for positive values, so it became the default for hidden layers in deep networks.

At the output you pick the activation that matches the question. Sigmoid gives one probability for a yes or no question. Softmax turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1, one per class; it is also what an LLM uses to choose its next token.

Two practical details. First, softmax has a numerical trap: exp of a big score, such as exp(1000), overflows to infinity, and infinity divided by infinity gives not-a-number. Softmax does not change if you subtract the same number from every score, so real code subtracts the largest score first. The largest exponent then becomes exp(0) = 1 and nothing overflows. Library functions (torch.softmax, and the softmax inside CrossEntropyLoss) already do this; you need it when you write softmax yourself, and the transformer lesson does exactly that.

Second, newer models rarely use plain ReLU. GELU and SiLU (also called swish) are smooth versions: they let small negative values through a little instead of cutting them to zero, and they are the usual choice in transformers and many modern networks. If a model card says GELU or SiLU, read it as ReLU with a gentle curve.
replace_subtopics.example: A clinic triage model scores a message for three queues: urgent 2.0, routine 1.0, admin 0.1. Softmax turns these into 66 percent, 24 percent and 10 percent. The model routes to urgent, and the 66 percent can be shown to staff as a confidence. A hand-written softmax over scores of 1000, 999 and 990 gives not-a-number until the maximum is subtracted; then it returns 73 percent, 27 percent and almost nothing.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

z = np.array([-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0])   # raw scores before activation

sigmoid = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))     # squashes to 0..1
tanh = np.tanh(z)                  # squashes to -1..1
relu = np.maximum(0, z)            # negatives become 0

print("sigmoid", sigmoid.round(3))
print("tanh   ", tanh.round(3))
print("relu   ", relu)

# softmax turns a list of scores into probabilities that sum to 1
scores = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
probs = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum()
print("softmax", probs.round(3), "sum", probs.sum().round(3))

# Output:
# sigmoid [0.047 0.269 0.5   0.731 0.953]
# tanh    [-0.995 -0.762  0.     0.762  0.995]
# relu    [0. 0. 0. 1. 3.]
# softmax [0.659 0.242 0.099] sum 1.0

# Softmax overflows for big scores unless you subtract the maximum first.
big = np.array([1000.0, 999.0, 990.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    naive = np.exp(big) / np.exp(big).sum()          # exp(1000) is infinity
print("naive ", naive)
shifted = np.exp(big - big.max())                    # same answer, no overflow
print("stable", (shifted / shifted.sum()).round(3))

# The modern smooth cousins of ReLU used in transformers
gelu = z * 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (z + 0.044715 * z ** 3)))  # tanh form
silu = z / (1 + np.exp(-z))                          # also called swish
print("gelu", gelu.round(3))
print("silu", silu.round(3))

# Output:
# naive  [nan nan nan]
# stable [0.731 0.269 0.   ]
# gelu [-0.004 -0.159  0.     0.841  2.996]
# silu [-0.142 -0.269  0.     0.731  2.858]

replace_subtopics.title: Training: optimizers, batches and epochs
replace_subtopics.body:
Gradient descent repeats three moves: forward pass, backward pass, update each weight by minus learning rate times gradient. The learning rate is the step size. Too big and the loss bounces or explodes; too small and training crawls.

Computing the gradient over millions of examples for every step is slow, so we use batches: small random groups, often 32 to 256 examples. One update per batch is stochastic gradient descent (SGD). One full pass over every batch is an epoch, and training typically runs for many epochs.

Adam is the most common optimizer today. It keeps a running average of recent gradients (momentum, so steps keep a steady direction) and of their size (so each weight gets its own step scale). It usually works with little tuning, often starting at a learning rate of 0.001.

The code trains a 2-4-1 network on XOR, the problem a perceptron cannot solve. With random seed 1 it reaches near-perfect predictions. With seed 0 the same code stalls at a loss of about 0.35, stuck with two predictions at 0.5, which shows that starting weights matter and why people rerun or use better optimizers.

Three more things appear in almost every real training config. The first is a learning-rate schedule: instead of one fixed step size, the rate changes during training. Warmup starts tiny and rises over the first few hundred steps, because early gradients are noisy and a big step can wreck the network. Cosine decay then lowers the rate smoothly toward zero so the last steps are fine adjustments. ReduceLROnPlateau is a simpler option: halve the rate whenever the validation loss stops improving. If a fine-tuning file says warmup_ratio or lr_scheduler_type, this is what it controls.

The second is the vanishing and exploding gradient problem. Backpropagation multiplies many small factors together, one per layer. In a deep network, if the factors are below 1 (sigmoid and tanh have slopes under 1 and flatten out) the gradient shrinks toward zero and the early layers stop learning; if they are above 1 it blows up. The output of the second example shows the first layer of a 12-layer network getting a gradient orders of magnitude smaller with sigmoid than with ReLU. Three remedies are standard: ReLU-family activations, careful weight initialisation (the starting weights are scaled by the layer width, as in the Xavier and He schemes that PyTorch layers use by default), and normalisation layers.

The third is gradient clipping. If one batch produces a gigantic gradient, one update can throw the weights far away. clip_grad_norm_ rescales all gradients so their combined size never exceeds a limit, typically 1.0. It is a cheap safety net that most transformer training scripts include.
replace_subtopics.example: A parcel company, Brisklane, trains a delay predictor on 400,000 past deliveries with batches of 256. That is about 1,563 updates per epoch. After 10 epochs the validation loss stops improving, so the team stops there instead of the 50 epochs they had planned. The Brisklane team also switched on 500 steps of warmup and cosine decay, after a run in which the loss suddenly jumped to not-a-number at step 90; adding gradient clipping at 1.0 stopped it from happening again.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([[0], [1], [1], [0]], dtype=float)   # XOR: 1 when inputs differ

W1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)); b1 = np.zeros(4)   # 2 inputs -> 4 hidden
W2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)); b2 = np.zeros(1)   # 4 hidden -> 1 output
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
lr = 1.0

for epoch in range(3001):
    # forward pass
    h = np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1)
    p = sig(h @ W2 + b2)
    loss = -np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))
    # backward pass (chain rule, layer by layer)
    dz2 = (p - y) / len(X)              # gradient at output score
    dW2 = h.T @ dz2; db2 = dz2.sum(0)
    dh = dz2 @ W2.T * (1 - h ** 2)      # back through tanh
    dW1 = X.T @ dh; db1 = dh.sum(0)
    # gradient descent update
    W1 -= lr * dW1; b1 -= lr * db1
    W2 -= lr * dW2; b2 -= lr * db2
    if epoch % 1000 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:4d}  loss {loss:.4f}")

print("predictions", p.ravel().round(3))

# Output:
# epoch    0  loss 0.6712
# epoch 1000  loss 0.0024
# epoch 2000  loss 0.0012
# epoch 3000  loss 0.0008
# predictions [0.    0.999 0.999 0.001]

# ---- Second example (PyTorch): learning-rate schedule, vanishing gradients, clipping ----
import torch
from torch import nn

# 1. Learning-rate schedule: warm up, then cosine decay
model = nn.Linear(4, 1)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
warm, total = 5, 20
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(
    opt, lambda s: (s + 1) / warm if s < warm
    else 0.5 * (1 + torch.cos(torch.tensor(3.14159265 * (s - warm) / (total - warm))).item()))
lrs = []
for step in range(total):
    opt.step()                       # (a real loop computes the loss and calls backward first)
    lrs.append(opt.param_groups[0]["lr"])
    sched.step()
print("lr at steps 0, 4, 12, 19:", [f"{lrs[i]:.5f}" for i in (0, 4, 12, 19)])

# 2. Vanishing gradients: same 12-layer net, sigmoid versus ReLU
def first_layer_grad(act):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    layers = []
    for _ in range(12):
        layers += [nn.Linear(32, 32), act()]
    net = nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(32, 1))
    loss = net(torch.randn(64, 32)).pow(2).mean()
    loss.backward()
    return net[0].weight.grad.norm().item()
print("gradient size at layer 1, sigmoid:", f"{first_layer_grad(nn.Sigmoid):.1e}")
print("gradient size at layer 1, ReLU:   ", f"{first_layer_grad(nn.ReLU):.1e}")

# 3. Gradient clipping: cap the total gradient size before the update
net = nn.Linear(32, 1)
net(torch.randn(8, 32) * 50).pow(2).mean().backward()
before = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(net.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)   # returns the size before clipping
after = sum(p.grad.norm() ** 2 for p in net.parameters()) ** 0.5
print(f"grad norm before {before:.0f}, after clipping {after:.1f}")

# Output:
# lr at steps 0, 4, 12, 19: ['0.00020', '0.00100', '0.00055', '0.00001']
# gradient size at layer 1, sigmoid: 4.5e-12
# gradient size at layer 1, ReLU:    1.4e-06
# grad norm before 5929, after clipping 1.0

replace_subtopics.title: Overfitting controls and PyTorch
replace_subtopics.body:
A big network can memorise its training data, including the noise, and then fail on new data. That is overfitting (see mlbasics). You spot it when training loss keeps falling while validation loss, measured on held-out data, starts rising.

Three controls are used almost everywhere. Early stopping watches validation loss and stops training, keeping the best checkpoint, once it has not improved for a set number of epochs (the patience). Dropout randomly switches off a fraction of hidden units on each training step, so the network cannot rely on any single unit; it is turned off when predicting. Weight decay adds a small pull toward zero on every weight, which keeps the model simpler; AdamW is Adam with weight decay applied in the recommended way. More data and data augmentation (for example flipping images) help too.

In practice nobody writes backprop by hand. PyTorch builds the network from layers, computes gradients with loss.backward(), and applies the optimizer with opt.step(). The example below is the XOR network again with all three controls. The code was run with PyTorch 2.x and its real output is shown at the end; with torch installed (pip install torch) you can reproduce it.

One more tool sits between overfitting and training speed: normalisation layers. As numbers pass through many layers their scale drifts, which makes training unstable. A normalisation layer rescales them to a steady average of 0 and spread of 1, then lets the network learn its own scale and shift. Batch normalisation (BatchNorm) does this for each feature across the examples in a batch; it speeds up training of image networks and gives a mild regularising effect, but it depends on batch size and behaves differently in eval mode, which uses stored running averages. Layer normalisation (LayerNorm) works within a single example across its features, so it does not depend on the batch at all; that is why transformers use it, and the transformer lesson assumes you know it. Rule of thumb: BatchNorm for image networks, LayerNorm for text and sequence models.
replace_subtopics.example: Wrenholt Components trained a sensor model whose validation loss was lowest at epoch 14 but training continued to epoch 60. Test accuracy was 81 percent. Turning on early stopping with patience 5, dropout 0.2 and weight decay 0.0001 kept the epoch 14 weights and test accuracy rose to 86 percent. Wrenholt's image-defect network also gained BatchNorm layers between its convolutions, and training reached the same accuracy in about half the epochs.

# Requires torch (pip install torch). Output below is from a real run.
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(0)

X = torch.tensor([[0., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 0.], [1., 1.]])
y = torch.tensor([[0.], [1.], [1.], [0.]])

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 8), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Dropout(p=0.1),        # dropout: silence 10% of hidden units while training
    nn.Linear(8, 1),          # one raw score (a logit) per example
)
loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()   # sigmoid plus cross-entropy, done stably
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=0.05, weight_decay=1e-4)

best, waited = float("inf"), 0
for epoch in range(3000):
    model.train()
    opt.zero_grad()                # clear last step's gradients
    loss = loss_fn(model(X), y)    # forward pass and loss
    loss.backward()                # backpropagation, done for you
    opt.step()                     # Adam update with weight decay
    model.eval()                   # dropout off for checking
    with torch.no_grad():          # use a separate validation set in real work
        val = loss_fn(model(X), y).item()
    if val < best - 1e-4:
        best, waited = val, 0
    else:
        waited += 1
    if waited >= 200:              # early stopping: no progress for 200 epochs
        break
print("stopped at epoch", epoch, "best loss", round(best, 4))
model.eval()
print(torch.sigmoid(model(X)).ravel().detach().numpy().round(3))

# Output (seed 0, CPU):
# stopped at epoch 853 best loss 0.0002
# [0. 1. 1. 0.]

print("batch norm, mean per feature:        ", bn(h).mean(0).detach().numpy().round(2))

add_subtopics.title: Generative and multimodal architectures
add_subtopics.body:
So far the architectures learned to label or predict. Generative architectures create new content, and multimodal ones connect different kinds of data such as text, images and sound. An FDE meets them in image generation, visual search, document photos and voice agents. The multimodal topic goes deeper; this section gives the core ideas.

An autoencoder has two halves. The encoder squeezes an input into a short vector, the bottleneck. The decoder tries to rebuild the original from that vector. Training minimises the rebuild error. The bottleneck is forced to keep only what matters, so it works as compression, as a way to learn features, and, because unusual inputs rebuild badly, as an anomaly detector (see anomaly).

Diffusion models make images. Training takes a real image, adds noise a little at a time until only static remains, and teaches a network to undo one small step of the noise. To generate, start from pure noise and apply the learned denoising step many times, guided by a text prompt, until a picture appears. Most current image generators work this way.

CLIP-style models train an image encoder and a text encoder together so that a photo and its caption land close together in one shared vector space. You can then search photos with words, or classify images with labels you never trained on, using the same cosine similarity you meet in embeddings.

Speech models are also transformers. Automatic speech recognition (ASR), such as Whisper, turns audio into text; text-to-speech (TTS) does the reverse. A voice agent chains ASR, an LLM, and TTS, and the delay of each step adds up.
add_subtopics.example: Fernhill Retail wanted shoppers to search its catalogue by describing a photo, such as 'green raincoat with a hood'. The FDE used a CLIP-style model to embed all 40,000 product photos once, embedded each search phrase at query time, and returned the nearest photos by cosine similarity. No training was needed. For a voice ordering line they chained Whisper-style speech recognition, an LLM and text-to-speech, and measured the delay of each step against a one-second target.

import numpy as np, torch
from torch import nn
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

torch.manual_seed(0)
X = torch.tensor(load_digits().data / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)   # 1,797 images of 64 pixels

# 1. Autoencoder: squeeze 64 numbers into 8, then rebuild them
enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 8))      # encoder
dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 64))      # decoder
opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(enc.parameters()) + list(dec.parameters()), lr=0.01)
for step in range(300):
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = ((dec(enc(X)) - X) ** 2).mean()       # how badly did we rebuild the image?
    loss.backward(); opt.step()
print("autoencoder rebuild error:", round(loss.item(), 4), "versus", round(X.var().item(), 4), "for guessing the average")

# 2. Diffusion, the forward half: blend an image with more and more noise
img = X[0]
noise = torch.randn_like(img)
for keep in (1.0, 0.7, 0.3, 0.0):       # share of the original signal that remains
    noisy = keep ** 0.5 * img + (1 - keep) ** 0.5 * noise
    corr = np.corrcoef(noisy.numpy(), img.numpy())[0, 1]
    print(f"signal kept {keep:.1f}: similarity to the original {corr:.2f}")

# 3. CLIP-style search: text and images live in the SAME vector space (made-up vectors)
image_vecs = {"photo of a red bicycle": np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.2]),
              "photo of a blue kettle": np.array([0.1, 0.9, 0.3])}
text_vec = np.array([0.8, 0.2, 0.1])      # the text "a red bike"
for name, v in image_vecs.items():
    cos = text_vec @ v / (np.linalg.norm(text_vec) * np.linalg.norm(v))
    print(f"{name}: cosine {cos:.2f}")

# Output:
# autoencoder rebuild error: 0.0207 versus 0.1414 for guessing the average
# signal kept 1.0: similarity to the original 1.00
# signal kept 0.7: similarity to the original 0.41
# signal kept 0.3: similarity to the original 0.12
# signal kept 0.0: similarity to the original -0.13
# photo of a red bicycle: cosine 0.99
# photo of a blue kettle: cosine 0.37

replace_subtopics.title: Attention and the jump to transformers
replace_subtopics.body:
Attention was first added to RNN translators around 2014 to remove the bottleneck. Instead of relying on one summary vector, the decoder could look back at every input word and decide how much each one mattered for the word it was writing.

The mechanism is simple. Each token asks a question (a query vector), every token offers a label (a key vector), and the dot product of query and key says how relevant they are. Softmax turns those scores into weights that add up to 1, and the output is a weighted blend of the tokens' value vectors. In the toy code, the word 'bank' gives most weight to itself, then to 'loan' and 'river', and least to 'the'.

In 2017 the paper 'Attention Is All You Need' dropped recurrence entirely. The transformer uses only attention plus small dense layers, so every token in a sequence is processed at the same time. That made training massively parallel on GPUs, which allowed much bigger models on much more data. This architecture underlies today's LLMs and many vision models. The transformer topic walks through one forward pass in detail.

A variation you will see in model cards is the mixture of experts (MoE). Instead of one big dense block after attention, the layer holds several smaller expert blocks and a small router that picks a few of them for each token. Only the chosen experts do any work for that token. The model card then lists two sizes: total parameters (everything stored) and active parameters (used per token). Speed and cost per token follow the active number, while the memory needed to load the model follows the total number. So an MoE model can be as knowledgeable as a much larger dense model yet cost about as much per token as a smaller one, but it still needs a big GPU (or several) to hold all the experts.
replace_subtopics.example: In 'she paid the bank before walking by the river bank', attention lets each 'bank' look at 'paid' or 'river' directly, however far away they are, to work out which meaning applies. An RNN would have to carry that clue step by step through every word in between. When Ravelsby read a model card that said '47B total, 13B active', they learned it would generate tokens about as fast as a 13B model but would still need memory for all 47B parameters.

import numpy as np

# Four words, each already turned into a 3-number vector (made-up values)
words = ["the", "bank", "river", "loan"]
vecs = np.array([[0.1, 0.0, 0.1],
                 [0.9, 0.8, 0.1],
                 [0.2, 0.9, 0.0],
                 [0.9, 0.1, 0.8]])

query = vecs[1]                          # "bank" asks: who is relevant to me?
scores = vecs @ query / np.sqrt(3)       # dot product with every word, scaled
weights = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum()   # softmax to percentages
context = weights @ vecs                 # blend of all words, by weight

for w, a in zip(words, weights):
    print(f"{w:6s} attention {a:.2f}")
print("new vector for 'bank':", context.round(2))

# Output:
# the    attention 0.16
# bank   attention 0.34
# river  attention 0.25
# loan   attention 0.26
# new vector for 'bank': [0.6  0.52 0.26]

# Mixture of experts: total versus active parameters
experts, active_per_token = 8, 2            # 8 expert blocks, 2 chosen for each token
expert_params = 5.6e9                       # parameters in each expert block (made-up round numbers)
shared_params = 1.6e9                       # attention layers and other parts every token uses
total = shared_params + experts * expert_params
active = shared_params + active_per_token * expert_params
print(f"total {total / 1e9:.1f}B parameters, active per token {active / 1e9:.1f}B")
print(f"memory must hold all {total / 1e9:.1f}B; compute per token is that of a {active / 1e9:.1f}B model")

replace_subtopics.title: GPUs and why they matter
replace_subtopics.body:
Almost all the work in a neural network is multiplying matrices: huge grids of weights times vectors of inputs. Each output number is independent of the others, so they can all be computed at the same time.

A CPU has a handful of powerful cores designed for varied, step-by-step work. A GPU (graphics processing unit) has thousands of simpler cores designed to do the same arithmetic on many numbers at once, plus very fast memory. For matrix maths a data-centre GPU is often tens to hundreds of times faster than a CPU. The 2012 image model AlexNet was trained on two gaming GPUs, and that result helped start the deep learning boom.

Three numbers dominate planning. Compute: generating one token costs roughly two operations per parameter, and this maths is what limits training and the reading of a long prompt (prefill), where thousands of tokens are processed together. Memory: all the weights must fit in the GPU's memory. Memory bandwidth: when one user is generating one token at a time (decoding), the chip must read every weight from memory for each token, so the limit is how fast memory can be read, not how fast it can multiply. A 7 billion parameter model in 16-bit is 14 GB, so a laptop reading at about 50 GB per second needs roughly 0.3 seconds per token, while a data-centre GPU reading at about 3,000 GB per second needs about 5 milliseconds. That is why a fast GPU feels so different, and why batching many users together is efficient: one read of the weights serves all of them.

Quantisation means storing each weight in fewer bits. 16-bit uses 2 bytes per weight, 8-bit uses 1 byte and 4-bit uses half a byte. A 7 billion parameter model shrinks from 14 GB to 7 GB to 3.5 GB, usually with a small quality loss that you should test on your own task. Less memory to read also means faster decoding.

The attention cache (the KV cache) is extra memory that grows with the length of the context and with the number of requests served at once: about layers x 2 x key-value size per token, times tokens, times batch size. Long contexts and many users can need more memory than the weights themselves. Training needs several times more memory than inference because gradients and optimizer state are stored too. This is why quantisation, smaller models and hosted APIs matter so much in practice.
replace_subtopics.example: Ravelsby Insurance asked why their laptop took minutes per answer from an open 7 billion parameter model. The reason is memory bandwidth: every token needs the 14 GB of weights read once, about 0.3 seconds per token on a laptop CPU, against about 5 ms on a data-centre GPU. The pure arithmetic (14 ms per token on a strong CPU, 0.05 ms on a GPU) is far smaller than the time spent reading memory. The 14 GB of weights would also not fit on their small office GPU, and a 4-bit version (3.5 GB) would fit but needed a quality test. Moving to a hosted endpoint was the practical answer.

# Rough compute to run a model: about 2 floating point operations
# (a multiply and an add) per parameter for each token processed.
params = 7e9                  # a 7 billion parameter model
flops_per_token = 2 * params

cpu_flops = 1e12              # example: ~1 TFLOP/s for a strong CPU
gpu_flops = 300e12            # example: ~300 TFLOP/s for a data-centre GPU

# The maths matters for training and for reading a long prompt (prefill).
for name, speed in [("CPU", cpu_flops), ("GPU", gpu_flops)]:
    ms = flops_per_token / speed * 1000
    print(f"{name}: {ms:.2f} ms of pure maths per token")

# Decoding one token for one user must read ALL the weights from memory.
weights_gb = params * 2 / 1e9            # 16-bit = 2 bytes per weight
print("weights in 16-bit:", weights_gb, "GB")
for name, gb_per_s in [("laptop CPU (~50 GB/s)", 50), ("data-centre GPU (~3000 GB/s)", 3000)]:
    print(f"{name}: about {weights_gb / gb_per_s * 1000:.0f} ms per token (memory-bound)")

# Quantisation: bytes per weight for 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit
for bits in (16, 8, 4):
    print(f"{bits}-bit: {params * bits / 8 / 1e9:.1f} GB for 7B, {70e9 * bits / 8 / 1e9:.0f} GB for 70B")

# KV cache: 2 (keys and values) x layers x key-value heads x head size x bytes, per token
layers, kv_heads, head_dim, bytes_each = 32, 8, 128, 2      # a typical 7B-class design
per_token = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_each
for tokens, batch in [(4_000, 1), (32_000, 1), (32_000, 8)]:
    print(f"context {tokens:>6,} x batch {batch}: {per_token * tokens * batch / 1e9:.1f} GB of cache")

# Output:
# CPU: 14.00 ms of pure maths per token
# GPU: 0.05 ms of pure maths per token
# weights in 16-bit: 14.0 GB
# laptop CPU (~50 GB/s): about 280 ms per token (memory-bound)
# data-centre GPU (~3000 GB/s): about 5 ms per token (memory-bound)
# 16-bit: 14.0 GB for 7B, 140 GB for 70B
# 8-bit: 7.0 GB for 7B, 70 GB for 70B
# 4-bit: 3.5 GB for 7B, 35 GB for 70B
# context  4,000 x batch 1: 0.5 GB of cache
# context 32,000 x batch 1: 4.2 GB of cache
# context 32,000 x batch 8: 33.6 GB of cache

add_glossary: Autoencoder
A network that squeezes input into a short vector and rebuilds it; large rebuild error can flag unusual inputs.
Diffusion model
An image generator trained to remove noise step by step; generation starts from pure noise.
CLIP
A model family that places images and text in one shared vector space so words can search pictures.
ASR / TTS
Automatic speech recognition (audio to text) and text-to-speech (text to audio).
Mixture of experts (MoE)
A layer with several expert blocks where a router uses only a few per token, so active parameters are fewer than total parameters.
Active parameters
The parameters actually used for one token in a mixture-of-experts model; they set the compute cost per token.
Quantisation
Storing weights in fewer bits (8 or 4 instead of 16) to save memory and speed decoding, at a small quality cost.
KV cache
Memory holding the keys and values of earlier tokens so they are not recomputed; it grows with context length and batch size.
Memory bandwidth
How fast data can be read from memory; it limits token speed when one user is decoding.
